Supporto telefono per bicicletta e moto - versione 2.0 Questa è una nuova versione del supporto telefono che ho progettato qualche mese fa ( https://makerworld.com/it/models/2877387-phone-holder-for-bicycle-motorcycle-scooter#profileId-3213255 ). Ho migliorato un po' l'estetica e ho reso più pratico l'aggancio e lo sgancio quando si cambia l'orientamento del telefono. Rispetto al modello precedente che era fatto di soli tre pezzi, per quello attuale ho scelto di separare le graffe che avvolgono il telefono, stampandole in modo che la trazione a cui sono sottoposte agisca nel senso della lunghezza del filamento, invece che dei layer sovrapposti. Ho introdotto una nuova molla elicoidale, che migliora l'apertura delle due parti laterali, e aumentato l'infill al 90% per gli snodi e le leve di serraggio. Per unire le diverse parti ho utilizzato sia i ganci a scatto già presenti nel precedente modello, sia un nuovo sistema di inserimento con profilo a coda di rondine e bloccaggio a fine corsa. Descrizione del modello Il supporto telefono è composto da 7 particolari: morsetto di fissaggio al manubrio base fissa del supporto base mobile leva di serraggio molla elicoidale graffe laterali “A” (2 pezzi) graffe inferiori “B” (2 pezzi) Il morsetto snodato si applica al manubrio della bicicletta o della moto. L’apertura è regolabile e si adatta a barre con diametro compreso tra circa 18 e 22 mm. Per migliorare l’aderenza sulla superficie liscia del manubrio, è previsto l’utilizzo di un comune elastico di gomma, come mostrato nelle istruzioni di montaggio. Il serraggio iniziale avviene tramite la vite integrata nel morsetto; una volta raggiunta la presa corretta, il bloccaggio finale viene fatto con la leva a scatto. L'estremità del morsetto va inserita in una delle due basi del supporto per mezzo di due profili a coda di rondine, permettendo di scegliere l’orientamento del telefono in verticale o in orizzontale. La due basi scorrono tra di loro per mezzo di una guida e una barra filettata che consente la regolazione della distanza fra le graffe laterali, in base alle dimensioni dello smartphone. La barra è dotata di una leva con eccentrico e molla di contrasto per il blocco e sblocco rapido, così da poter inserire e rimuovere il telefono in modo pratico. Caratteristiche principali Supporto telefono per bici, scooter e moto leggere Morsetto regolabile per manubri da circa 18 a 22 mm Orientamento del telefono verticale o orizzontale Larghezza regolabile in base allo smartphone Leva di blocco e sblocco rapido Nessun attrezzo necessario per il montaggio Solo parti in stampa 3D, nessun altro componente in metallo Design ottimizzato per aumentare resistenza a trazione Materiali e attrezzi necessari Per completare l’assemblaggio è sufficiente aggiungere un comune elastico di gomma con diametro indicativo di circa 30-40 mm. Non sono necessari attrezzi. Consigli di stampa Il supporto è stato progettato per poter sfruttare al massimo le caratteristiche di resistenza nel senso della lunghezza del filamento, anche con materiali poco performanti. Io l'ho stampato con un comune PLA e l'ho testato sulla mia bici. Per renderlo ancora più robusto, ad esempio per l'utilizzo su moto, si può stampare in PETG, o, per chi ha stampanti più performanti della mia A1, anche in PET, ABS o PC. Istruzioni di montaggio 1. Assemblaggio dei particolari Dopo aver stampato tutti i particolari, rimuovere i supporti delle parti a sbalzo ed eliminare le piccole imperfezioni, aiutandosi se necessario con una limetta per unghie. Avvitare e svitare completamente un paio di volte le barre filettate, per eliminare gli impuntamenti. Inserire le graffe laterali “A” negli inserti a coda di rondine delle basi, spingere a fondo fino a che si avverte il “clic” del bloccaggio. Inserire i ganci delle graffe inferiori “B” nei fori delle basi, applicando una pressione uniforme (si, ci vuole parecchia forza, è normale) Accoppiare fra loro le due basi, inserendo la guida, la barra filettata e la molla. Basta avvitare la barra solo per pochi millimetri, la regolazione finale sarà fatta in seguito in base alle dimensioni del telefono. 2. Montaggio del morsetto sul manubrio Aprire lo snodo del morsetto e agganciare l’elastico di gomma tra il filetto della vite e l’estremità opposta del morsetto, facendogli fare mezza torsione in modo che rimanga in posizione. Inserire il morsetto aperto sotto il manubrio e, mentre lo si richiude, sfilare l’elastico dall’estremità opposta e agganciarlo al filetto della vite, vicino all’altro capo. Avvicinare tra loro le due estremità del morsetto e iniziare a serrare la vite girando la leva di bloccaggio. Non serrare subito a fondo: quando il morsetto inizia a fare presa sul manubrio, utilizzare la leva a scatto per il bloccaggio definitivo. Verificare che a morsetto montato, la scritta “UP” sia in alto. 2. Aggancio e sgancio del supporto A seconda che si voglia orientare il telefono in orizzontale o verticale, inserire dall'alto il supporto sul morsetto, utilizzando gli scassi a coda di rondine presenti su una o sull'altra base. Far scorrere verso il basso il supporto, fino a che si avverte il “clic” del bloccaggio. Se si desidera cambiare l'orientamento del telefono, basta tirare verso l'alto il supporto, tenendo fermo il morsetto, sfilarlo e inserirlo nello scasso dell'altra base. 3. Regolazione apertura e blocco del telefono Iniziare a serrare la barra filettata per avvicinare le graffe laterali. Inserire il telefono e continuare la regolazione fino a lasciare lo spazio sufficiente per poterlo estrarre facilmente. Verificare infine che il telefono venga bloccato correttamente agendo sulla leva. Note di sicurezza Prima di usare il supporto su strada, verificare sempre che tutte le parti siano ben agganciate, che il morsetto sia stabile sul manubrio e che il telefono sia trattenuto correttamente. Trattandosi di un oggetto stampato in 3D, la resistenza finale dipende dal materiale utilizzato, dalle impostazioni di stampa e dalla qualità della stampa stessa. Per maggiore sicurezza, soprattutto su moto, scooter o strade sconnesse, consiglio di usare anche un laccetto o un sistema di sicurezza aggiuntivo per evitare la caduta accidentale dello smartphone.

description: This model is the third in a series of “Thinline Scale Model” structure kits for Z-scale and N-scale model railroading. [Note: the HO-scale version of this kit is available here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/3036818-the-trackside-factory-ho-scale-edition#profileId-3414170 .] The Trackside Factory (TSM#03) - This structure kit is for a factory that could be located off of a track siding. For my layout, this factory will be receiving lumber from a lumber mill down the line and producing wood-based products, such as furniture, for shipping out to market via the railroad. To see other kits in this series, including HO-scale versions, please visit my collection page: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/15297762-model-train-projects . I designed this model in SolidWorks inspired by an original design by a former member of our Z-scale modeling club - he did market a laser-cut wood kit for a short while (as fannocreek designs ) but alas those kits are no longer available so he graciously gave me permission to craft my model as a likeness of his . Given my model is for 3d-printing, I've completely re-engineered the way that the kit is made and assembled, and I've made other design changes based on how some interior aspects of the factory would change some of the exterior appearance. And, after many failed attempts to recreate an exposed support structure under the trackside dock and front deck that would print reliably in one piece, I chose to enclose the underside of both dock and deck. Important Note: Before proceeding to print and build these kits, please note the following special requirements needed to produce good results. Also, please read through the entire description to understand all of the assembly steps required. For printing, a 0.2mm nozzle and a clean smooth build plate is required - this model is specifically designed for using a 0.08mm layer layer height and a 0.22mm line width for the Z-scale model. The N-scale model uses a 0.11mm layer height and a 0.22mm line width. This kit includes both two-color and three-color prints - an AMS is required. Supplied needed: fast setting (5-10 seconds) CA adhesive with a toothpick or tool for spreading along mating edges; and a selection of acrylic paints / brushes for painting the model (if desired). Tools needed: a good bed scraper tool for removing some of parts from the smooth build plate - I found the bed scraping blade supplied with the printers by Bambu Lab to work well for this purpose (most beneficial was its thin sharp blade for lifting very thin prints) . The Print Profiles - Three profiles each are available for each model train scale ( Z or N ) of this structure kit, the profiles generally differ by single ( P1S , A1 , H2S , etc.) and dual-nozzle ( H2D and H2C ) printers, and also an A1 Mini -specific profile. Please note that all of the profiles include a number of parameter changes from the standard print profiles that probably should not be tampered with if you want good results. One of the more important profile variances is that I've significantly slowed down the nozzle speed, travel speed and acceleration to help assure the best result printing the detail features of these models - I've specifically supplied separate profiles based on direct-drive nozzle count because changing the printer of a single-nozzle profile to a dual-nozzle printer (and vice versa) may cause the speed settings to be lost in the profile. I highly recommend that you use the appropriate single or dual-nozzle profile matching your printer capability, and I include the X2D with the single-nozzle printers since its auxiliary nozzle is not recommended for use with a 0.2mm nozzle . Important note regarding the factory name: The original laser-cut wood kit included decals for naming the factory, a choice of either “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” or “ TELLER & SONS MFG ”, the latter one being the one I'm planning to use on my Z-scale layout. For the Z-scale profiles, I've only included the “ TELLER & SONS MFG ” choice as the other name is too long to print cleanly. For the N-scale profiles, I've included both naming options with the “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” as the default choice - if you prefer “ TELLER & SONS MFG ” on your N-scale model, find the build plate where the wall with the name appears and deselect the named wall you don't want and select the named wall that you do want. Make sure that only one of these walls are selected for printing … if both are selected, Bambu Studio should complain and you will need to deselect one to proceed; if none are selected, you will be missing a wall in the print so make that one is selected. If you have questions about any of this, please feel free to reach out to me. One final note … you can optionally remove the name from the wall by deleting the text element, or you can attempt to change the name to something you prefer but please note that you should take care to recenter, left to right, the text on the wall after you edit the name. Also note that the text tool when used on a textured surface such as these walls can be a bit finicky with sometimes distorting the placement of individual characters so you might have to mess around with it a bit to get it to behave. I've taken some care to make sure that the text fits nicely when positioned vertically across the siding boards. And finally, most of the text fonts available will not print well at these scales which is why I've focused on the two sans-serif fonts used in the profile. Important note before removing the parts from the build plate: After printing your model, please only remove the parts after the build plate has completely cooled to room temperature. Many of the model parts are extremely thin (e.g., between 0.64 and 0.8mm in Z-scale ) and can be easily damaged. Some of the parts can't be removed simply by flexing the build plate so with the build plate removed from the printer and set firmly on a work surface, use a sharp bed scraper tool to very carefully work up and lift each individual part by working slowly around the edges of the part. When removing some of the smaller parts, such as the L-shaped awning supports, you may want to place your hand over to capture them as they will tend to fly off once released from the plate. Choosing Filaments - In my profiles, I've chosen to use Bambu Lab PLA Matte filaments as I prefer the surface finish over PLA Basic . With the model based on four colors as set in the profiles, all of the major elements of the model could be left as printed but there are a small number of details that I recommend be painted to help finish the model (see below for painting recommendations). I've tried to minimize the number of color changes needed on each build plate in the profiles to keep purge waste as low as possible. === ASSEMBLY INSTRUCTIONS === This diagram provides a general overview of the kit parts. The Z-scale and N-scale kits have the same set of parts - in terms of design, only the two small winch supports differ between the kits as the detail of the N-scale supports could not be reliably replicated in Z-scale. While these instructions are illustrated with pictures of the N-scale kit, the instructions are the same for the Z-scale kit. === Painting and Window Glazing Recommendations === At a minimum, I would suggest adding some diluted color washes to give a more weathered look to the structure. Before assembling the kits in the photos, I choose to paint the lower masonry block surfaces of the two white bases to help bring out the detail. I first coated the masonry surfaces with a white acrylic gesso and after that dried thoroughly, I worked it over with a thinned coat of ‘tarnished’ black, the gesso helps to create a more receptive surface for the paint on the plastic. For those interested, here is an Amazon link to the Micro-Mark Acrylic paints I've used on my models: https://a.co/d/0fMC2PB2 . There are a number of details in this kit that should be painted prior to assembly. This include the two chimneys, the utility cabinet, the shipping crates, and the firebox as seem in the following photo. The firebox is an integrated feature of the middle wall and it takes a bit of extra care in painting it without getting paint on the wall siding (blue) - note that I chose to paint the lid in gray with the rest of the box in red. For the crates, I only chose to dirty them up a bit to help differentiate them from the dock color. Note: If you choose to change the filament colors to either reduce the number of filaments or simply to picking more neutral colors with a plan of painting the model, you should consider painting individual parts prior to assembly although adding weathering detail is often done with the overall model built up. Using some paint color washes can help enhance the details while also making the building not appear as it was just build yesterday :-). If you want to add window glazing (simulated window glass), I would suggest that being done either before attaching the walls to the base, or at least right after attaching the walls to the base - going beyond those steps in the assembly process will make it difficult to adding glazing. You also need to consider that if you are painting the model, care must be taken to not get paint on your window glazing so the painting versus glazing order becomes important. I'm still messing around with different techniques for glazing 3d-printed models … either using a clear film/plastic material or something like this clear adhesive by Microscale Industries ( https://a.co/d/0gy3e33L ) that can also be used to form small windows on models (this stuff can be a bit tricky to get it to work right but I've successfully used similar, unfortunately discontinued by Micro-Mark , products in the past. === Starting with some sub-assemblies === There are a number of sub-assemblies to complete prior to starting the general assembly of the kit. It is recommended that before applying adhesive, you study all of the photos closely to see how parts are supposed to fit once assembled. Once each is completed, set it aside until needed in the general assembly. The Fire Escape Note the alignment of the underside notches of the ladder to the support features of the wall - make sure to get the ladder in the proper orientation with the shorter piece of the ladder above the top notch and the longer piece of the ladder below the bottom notch (and extending below the wall once attached. Also take care to center the latter, left to right, on the provided supports. This can be a rather delicate job and using some tweezers might be helpful. Note the alignment of the escape platform with the two provided wall supports centered beween the platform leg structures. The Winch Support Beams The winch supports are two small parts that look somewhat like mini-tripods. Note the alignment of the winch support relative to the top of the door and the notch in the wall. The awning platforms with supports Note that the support legs have bumps that fit into the underside slots of the awning bases. Also note that the leg of the support is positioned closest to the thinner edge of the awning base. Key to this sub-assembly is to make sure that the supports sit flush against the surface of the base with the leg standing straight up, left to right, from the base. The larger awning platform is for the trackside dock and the smaller one is for the front deck. The clerestory Note that the four walls fit well within the inside cavity of the main roof beam base. Once they are in position with all of the wall edges lined up and with the walls firmly seated down within the cavity, add the adhesive drops where the walls meet and with a couple more at the base on the longer walls down where they meet the base, and hold everything in position, making sure not to disrupt that the wall edges appear properly aligned with no obvious gaps. The upper beam can then be added with adhesive on the small flat surfaces of the beam to glue to the inside of the end walls when set into the alignment gaps. The right-side chimney Note that the chimney needs to be inserted from the underside of the roof section and oriented with the thicker side of the chimney wedge base positioned toward the large gap side of the roof. Once you have the chimney firmly seated flush to the underside of the roof, apply some adhesive to hold it in place. The chimney wedged base serves to orient the chimney vertical once the roof is installed on the model. Now you should have the following sub-assemblies ready for use when starting the general assembly of the factory. === Assembling the factory === The base Each of the interlocking tabs on the left-side base, the trackside dock and the front deck have corresponding receiving slots on the right-side base, and for the dock and deck, also on the left-side base. Gently press each tab into its corresponding slot and work each in until its fully inserted and flush … it helps to place the assembly on a solid surface and press things down from the top but be careful to not damage any of the other features on the bases when doing this … I've strengthened the underside of the bases in the areas around the slots to facilitate pressing down in those areas. While these four parts are designed to hold together without need for gluing, you may choose to add some CA adhesive to the mating joints underneath once the parts are mated up flush together. The right-side walls Start with the middle wall … note the alignment notch position where the middle should lock into place. Make sure that the wall sits flush with the side of the stairway and other vertical features of the base. Next is the back wall … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and a mid-point along the bottom edge … if all goes according to plan, once in place, the edge between the middle and back walls should line up very nicely. Continue with the front wall … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and a mid-point along the bottom edge. Next is installing the second floor insert … note the orientation of the second floor insert and how it aligns at the top of the stairway. Apply adhesive drops at the tops of the vertical features of the base and then place the second floor insert within the structure and flush down on those features. After the floor is in place, you may choose to add some more adhesive to help secure the front and back walls to the second floor. Finally, adding the right-side wall sub-assembly with the fire escape … take care not to damage the ladder when handling this wall section. Again, apply small adhesive drops to the exposed surfaces where the wall will sit. The left-side walls Starting with the back wall, apply small adhesive drops where shown and assure that the wall is flush with the base alignment edge and vertical features once in place. Next, add the front wall ... Finally, add the left-side wall using the vertical surface of the fireplace feature for adhesive and as a supporting surface for the wall. The awnings Each awning sub-assembly has three slots that are designed to align with the three support tabs on the left-side front and back walls. To install each awning sub-assembly, gently press the slots over the corresponding tabs … make sure to not damage the awning support legs while doing this. I generally start with one of the end slots followed by the opposite end slot, making sure that the middle slot is in its proper place as I press them together. Place a finger inside the wall as support while pressing the awning base flush to the outside of the wall. No adhesive is needed at this point. Repeat with the awning against the back wall. Make sure that the awning bases are flush with the walls before proceeding … it may take some persuasion but do be careful to not damage anything while working them on. Now is time to install the awning top surfaces. Examine the awning surface parts closely … note that one of the long edges of each will have a complete shingle row and the other a partial one, the partial row should end up mounted close to the wall so that the complete row of shingles is exposed along the outer edge of the awning. Apply adhesive drops along the edges close to the wall and the outside edge of the awning. (If, as you move the awning surface pieces into place, a bit of adhesive gets pushed up into the crack where the awning base is pressed against the wall, that would not be a bad thing :o). Now it is time to add some adhesive to keep the awning legs in the proper place … for this, you will need either a toothpick or another way to gab a small drop of adhesive behind each of the legs where they will sit up against the leg alignment features of the dock and deck. Each leg should be positioned in front of and centered on each alignment bump … the legs are a bit flexible and move easily at this point so dab on a small drop of adhesive just behind the lower back portion of the leg and then move it into place followed by gently pressing down on the awning while the adhesive takes hold. Do this for each leg, one at a time until you have secured all three back-side legs followed by all three front-side legs. The roof support beams The left-side roof support beam fits within the notch at the top of the left-side wall and the beam support shelf of the middle wall. Once in position, make sure that the beam is sitting flush with the surfaces of the middle wall support shelf and the inside of the left-wall. The right-side clerestory sub-assembly also serves as the roof support beam for the main right-side roof sections. Apply adhesive to both ends where indicated and position the beam structure between the notches of the right-side front and back walls. Key to this step is making sure that the clesestory sub-assembly is sitting level/balanced between the walls … you should be able to judge it being level by observing how the roof support surfaces align evenly with the top edges of the walls on both sides. The roof sections For the left-side roof sections, note that the underside of each roof panel there are recessed areas that are intended to be positioned over the top edges of the walls being covered … there is no need to specifically align these recesses as the alignment of the roof sections are more dependent on getting the top edges of the roof panels snugly positioned under the beam's top finished surface as seen in the final image of this illustration. On the right side of our factory, the two main roof sections are designed to fit around the clerestory with the main roof section that has the factory chimney being mounted on the far right side. Take care to not damage the chimney when attaching that roof section. Finally, attach the remaining small roof sections to the top of the clerestory structure. Some final details The left-side chimney needs to be installed using a little bit of adhesive … make sure that the lower angled surface of the chimney sits flush with the exposed portion of the beam such that the chimney sits vertical on the roof. All that remains now are the shipping crates and the utility cabinet. You can see where I've chosen to position the utility cabinet on the side of the factory, using a small dot of adhesive on the upper back of the cabinet to hold it against the wall. Shipping crate placement is up to you … here are a couple of examples where the crates have been left on the trackside dock. I hope that copies of this model find good homes on model train layouts around the world … I have a spot on my Z-scale layout where Teller & Sons Manufacturing will definitely be doing business … if you are careful and patient, you should be able to produce a nice looking structure … have fun with it!

Hi everyone, this is a personal project of mine. Please read below for more details, and feel free to reach out if you need any help with this model. TLDR: A custom-built 4-DOF desktop robotic arm designed in Solidworks. Build : Turntable base (3D-printed ball bearing race, MG996R servo) → shoulder (MG996R) → elbow (SG90) → wrist (SG90) → gripper (fingers/lever reused from a GrabCAD reference, everything else original). Code : Arduino sketch, keyboard nudges servos via a generic moveServo(index, delta) function, parallel arrays for servos/pins/angles, constrain() for safety, recenter-to-90° key. No feedback or interrupts — kept deliberately simple. Hardware : Everything is intended to be assembled with M3 hardware, sizes up to you. Whatever works best. You will need 2 SG90 and 2 MG996R servos along with the various attachments. Servos can either be superglued or screwed directly into the plastic (I tried an iteration with holes, but the hold seemed worse than just screwing the screws directly into the plastic. DISCLAIMER: Size is often not consistent for these servos and their attachments. I bought some really cheap SG90s and they were way off from the spec I was expecting. This is why I have given you access to actual CAD models, as I highly recommend tinkering, making improvements, and customizing this model to your specs. Even in my models I just found publicly available servo models which did not exactly match the ones I bought. Robotic Arm A 4-DOF desktop robotic arm designed and built from scratch as a personal engineering project. All structural components were custom-modeled in SolidWorks and 3D printed, with servo geometry measured directly from physical hardware using digital calipers. The arm is capable of planar reach-and-grasp tasks within an approximate 15–20 cm workspace and is controlled via keyboard input over serial. CAD & Mechanical Design All structural components were designed from scratch in SolidWorks/Inventor, modeled from physical hardware measurements taken with digital calipers. The arm is a 4-DOF serial manipulator with a total reach of approximately 15–20 cm. Additionally, all parts were designed for M3 hardware. While those are not found in the model, please use M3 washers on the gripper and screws throughout to ensure the best fit. For servo attachments, use the provided screws and screw them directly in the plastic. I’ve experimented drilling into holes and drilling directly in the plastic, the latter holds significantly better. Base: The circular turntable base is fully custom-designed and integrates a 3D-printed ball bearing race using 1/8" diameter balls, enabling smooth continuous rotation driven by an MG996R servo. The two-tier disc profile houses the servo internally, keeping the footprint compact. Arm Links: The shoulder and elbow joints are custom-designed structural links. The shoulder is actuated by an MG996R servo for higher-torque lifting; the elbow uses an SG90. Joint geometry and servo mounting pockets were modeled directly from caliper measurements of the physical servos — as dimensions vary slightly between manufacturers, printed parts may require minor tolerance adjustment for servos from different suppliers. Wrist & Gripper: The wrist rotation is driven by an SG90. The gripper leverages the lever arm and finger geometry from an existing GrabCAD reference design ( gripper-servo-sg90-1 ) with direct reuse of those components, modified only to adjust mounting hole sizing for fit. All surrounding structure — wrist housing, servo mounts, and interface brackets — is original. Design Inspiration: Structural layout and proportions drew loose reference from a robotics arm with feeding spoon on GrabCAD. No geometry from that model was reused directly. Programming The arm is controlled via an Arduino Uno running a keyboard-control sketch written in Arduino IDE. Each keypress nudges the corresponding servo by a fixed angle step. The four joints are mapped to two-key pairs (increase/decrease) across the keyboard, with an additional key to recenter all servos to 90°. Servo state is managed using a Servo array alongside parallel pin and angle arrays, with a single generic moveServo(index, delta) function handling all joints. Angles are clamped with constrain() to prevent out-of-range writes. The architecture is intentionally minimal — no interrupt-driven input, no position feedback. In the future, if I have time, I will add a dual-sense controller mode since joysticks tend to feel more natural. Note : The circuit diagram provided comes directly from this project which makes a 6 DoF arm. The same logic applies for a 4 DoF arm, just make sure that you are not providing power to the servos directly from the Arduino as this can potentially fry the Uno. Another future iteration would be to change the elbow joint to a more powerful servo, as the SG90 can struggle with the load when lifting an object in addition to the weight of the arm

model_name: Fan Vertical Antenna V2 - Pole Mount, 10-40m
description: I like building antennas. This is an ongoing project and there have been major changes from V1 to V2. There may be more to come based on how it works. If you want a “sure-thing” and support - I'd recommend a DX Commander. Version 1 of this model had issues with the base deforming during high heat. I had updated that model with an improved base but have since reinforced it more based on AI analysis. There were a couple issues: PETG is apparently subject to “creep” if under tension the black PETG I used absorbed more heat allowing easier deformation the mechanical structure wasn't robust enough ASA is the recommended filament for this build. I'm still using PETG for two reasons: 1) I want to see how the improved mechanical design works, and 2) I haven't finished my external exhaust hookup so I can print ASA. I've also split it into two models - one for ground mount (as in V1) and added a pole mount option (this one). I've also added a number of support pieces that I'll reference later. Changes for V2: Even stronger base using design and printing modifications based on AI analysis of the CAD files Now supports permanent mounting on a pole in the ground (There will be a separate ground mount version) Wire hole diameter decreased - removed the need for small spacers New layer for guy ropes - SpiderBeam recommends a higher level guy rope. Since V1 was ground mounted I chose to move the guy ropes lower. This version adds a new layer consistent with SpiderBeam's recommendation Added a bird defender , holes on each layer to add filament that sticks up. It doesn't stop the birds from landing on the antenna and pooping on it, but it does seem to reduce it The base is designed to use ¼" by 1" stainless steel bolts. You'll also need washers, lock washers and nuts (11) ¼" x 1" stainless bolts (11) ¼" stainless lock washers (22) ¼" stainless washers (11) ¼" stainless wing nuts This uses a 12m Heavy Duty Spider Pole with the top two sections removed. For permanent mounting, you will need the “stay up” kit. You will also need stainless/marine grade ¼" ring terminals for wiring the driven elements, base driven elements, base ground elements and radials. A panel mount SO-239 is used. Note: when wiring it, have the wire make a complete loop (feed the driven elements in both directions). It will work otherwise but if you rewire wrong it de-tunes the antenna. When installing the plates, they can be above or below the “stay-up” clamps. When I got my second Spider Pole, I found differences in how tightly the plates fit. Push them as low as they will go on the appropriate section. If they are still a little loose and can rotate, put electrical tape on the side diameter to snug it up. For tuning, start with 40 meters. Disconnect the driven elements for all other bands while leaving them installed. Once 40m is tune, go higher in frequency band by band. NOTE: On the first version I couldn't get 10m to tune. I was able to tune it. The issue is that with harmonics its hard to tell which low is for the 10m element and which is just a harmonic. Before connecting the 10m element, use your NanoVNA to do a sweep from 1 MHz to 30 MHz using NanoVNASaver. Save that sweep as a reference. Connect the 10m element and do another sweep. It should identify a new low that is the one you would use for calculating the calibration for 10m. On V1 I had planned on it being used for field activations. I assumed I'd need to retune so I left the holes in the plates larger to allow zip ties to go through. Since this is intended for a permanent mount, I used smaller wire holes since you don't need zip ties. (I used zip ties while tuning, but once tuned I used adhesive heat shrink tubing to to hold the foldback). For the guy ropes, Kevlar line is recommended. I've used paracord but it needs regular adjusting due to stretching. I will update with my wire lengths the next time I take it down to tune. I used smaller lengths than the recommended lengths for the DX Commander Signature 9. Related models are: Wire Labels for the driven elements https://makerworld.com/en/models/1486447-pota-performer-18-gauge-wire-band-labels#profileId-1553134 “Sockets” to allow screw guy anchors to be below ground level allowing you to remove the guy rope and mow over the anchor https://makerworld.com/en/models/2986316-antenna-guy-anchor-recess#profileId-3351047 PVC pipe mount spacer (not uploaded yet) Grass deflector to keep grass from growing around the antenna base (not uploaded yet) Covers and plugs for 2" conduit https://makerworld.com/en/models/2986399-antenna-coax-conduit-2-schedule-40-pvc-cap#profileId-3351151 Coax labels for in the shack https://makerworld.com/en/models/2843997-coax-labels#profileId-3170941 I failed to take pictures of all the parts when I printed them. model_name: 26g Ultralight Mouse - Bambu Wireless Mouse Kit
description: Inspired by the zeromouse and finalmouse, this is a more accessible and affordable ultralight wireless mouse that uses the Bambu Wireless Mouse Components Kit. This is a size reduction of my other ultralight mouse . Check out that one if this is too small for you. The mouse buttons use a locking dovetail design, which means you can design your own buttons and hot swap them as you like. To install the ones in the print profile, clear the support material from the dovetail, then slide the button onto the mouse body from the front. The protrusion under the button face that actually engages with the PCB button needs to be toward the outside of the mouse on both sides. They should fit nice and easy if they are on the correct sides. If they are on the wrong sides, you will have to force them and will likely break the mouse body. I have included a profile for taller and even shorter buttons, but the ones in the main profile are my suggestion. There bambu kit needs to be modified slightly in order to make these parts fit correctly. The solder tab on the battery terminals needs to be folded in so that it bends slightly toward the spring/nub. This is a delicate operation that should be done carefully with pliers so the solder connection and wire are not broken from the tabs. This allows the contacts to be installed with the wires facing down, so the wires do not interfere with the hand grips. The small flared pieces of metal on either side of the nub/spring also need to be crushed down with pliers so they do not snag when being installed upside down. These wires need to be installed first, then the lens, followed by the board (with wheel preinstalled), before finally adding the finger buttons. This was designed to be used with dot skates like this . The skates from the normal bambu kit need to be cut in half to fit, and the cut corners need to be rounded. One goes under each button and one goes in each rear corner. IMPORTANT: The mouse will not function without the skid pads. It will slide perfectly fine on a mousepad, but the skid pads keep the laser the correct distance from the surface. Without them, the laser will not track correctly. I use these rechargeable lithium batteries so I dont go through AAAs too often. These batteries are lighter than a standard AAA and have USB-C ports in them to recharge them. If you are willing to do a bit of soldering, the Bambu PCB will accept standard 3 pin micro switches. The plastic finger button heights work for the stock Bambu buttons but should also work with standard 3 pin micro switches. I have tested with Huano blue shell pink dots and Kailh GM 8.0s as well and both work with the included finger buttons.

model_name: Tempest Putter - Low-Torque / Modular / High MOI
description: Tempest - A Modular 3D Printed Putter with Everything You Need Looking for a customizable putter without the price tag of today's premium designs? This project combines the flexibility of 3D printing with design features inspired by modern high-performance putters. The putter head is designed to incorporate removable weights, allowing the majority of the mass to be positioned around the perimeter. This increases the moment of inertia (MOI), helping improve stability on off-center strikes while reducing twisting through impact. One of the key features of this design is its modular construction. The shaft insert is a separate component that bolts into the main putter head, allowing different putter head designs to be swapped without needing to remove or reinstall the shaft. Simply remove a few screws, install a new head, and you're ready to go. The shaft insert has a lie angle of 74 degrees and a static loft angle of 3 degrees to match the feel of many center-shafted putters. The design of the head of the putter has been carefully made to ensure that the center of mass is aligned with the center of the face. It sits slightly in front of the center of the shaft, providing little torque when swinging. Therefore, the design of this putter naturally eliminates the majority of the torque that can open or close the face while putting. This can make it significantly easier to keep the face square at impact. To improve feel, the striking face is printed from TPU, providing a soft but responsive impact that closely resembles the insert faces found on many premium putters. Including the printed parts, added weights, screws, and epoxy, the total mass of the head of the putter is right around 320g. Features Large integrated putting alignment aids High-MOI perimeter-weighted design Center of Mass positioned to produce Low Torque when swinging Modular construction with interchangeable putter heads TPU face insert for a soft, responsive feel Removable shaft adapter secured with screws Designed for commonly available hardware and weights Inexpensive and creative alternative to traditional putters Hope you can have as much fun with this project as I did and get to give it a try out on course! For instructions, materials, and a list of parts to purchase/use, see the information below! Happy printing! Modular Design: Find other compatible putter heads here! Eclipse Putter - Low Torque / Modular / High MOI Material Selection Body / Shaft Insert - PETG is recommended for outdoor use and to withstand higher temperatures while being relatively easy to print. Face Insert - TPU provides a soft yet confident feel when striking the ball. Assembly Be sure to read all the following steps before beginning assembly of your putter! The order in which some of these steps are taken is very important! Print all required components in your favorite colors. Be sure to print each component in its recommended material. Support removal. This step can be rather difficult due to the way the model must be printed, so my recommendation is to work from the outside inwards. I've used normal supports for the flat-bottomed sections to allow for each of the gaps for the weights to be cleared in a singular piece. Press the TPU face into the putter body. Secure it by using super glue or epoxy. Install the weights. All weights should sit flat within the head of the putter when installed correctly. A total of 30 individual 0.25oz weights are to be inserted, with 4 stacked near the face and 2 stacked in all other locations. While removing the film on the weights (making them stick) is recommended, it is not required for the putter to work great. Doing so may reduce noises heard when making contact with the ball slightly but will make it more difficult to remove the weights if interchanging putter heads. Prior to installing the bottom plate, it can be helpful to lay a layer of tape over the bottom plate and cut to size. This will reduce some noise made when putting. Install the bottom plate to the putter head at the 5 holes around the perimeter. Ensure that the side which features cutouts matching the position of the weights is facing the inserted weights. Use 5x M3 x 3/8" wood screws (link provided below for the ones used). Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Cut down the putter shaft to your desired length (I cut mine down to 36in for my height). For a great step-by-step process to complete this, check out this YouTube video: How to Shorten a Putter with a Steel Shaft . Install the grip to your putter shaft. I recommend completing this step before installing the shaft adapter and putter head as there is less time to work and straighten out the grip in comparison. For a great guide to doing this, check out this other YouTube tutorial: How to Install a Putter Grip (jump to 3:00 in the video). Bolt the shaft adapter/insert into the putter head after sliding the shaft adapter into place from the top. Using 3x M3 x 3/8" wood screws, secure the bottom plate, main body, and adapter together through the bottom in the three central holes. Then, complete the installation by using one more screw in the hole near the top of the putter towards the back. Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Epoxy the shaft into the adapter by applying epoxy to the shaft and sliding it in from the top. The epoxy which is suggested has a long working time which allows you to rotate the putter shaft so the the grip precisely lines up with its correct orientation. My recommendation for alignment of the grip is as follows: look down the shaft and line up the flat part of the grip with the line on top of the putter which is parallel to the direction of your stroke. Once aligned properly, wipe away any excess epoxy from the top of the putter. Let the putter sit overnight so that the epoxy can fully cure. Next step, rolling putts! The Tomato System – Storm Edition The original Tomato System exceeded all expectations and quickly became one of my most popular gardening designs. It proved that a modular, stackable support system could be easy to print, easy to expand, and adaptable to a wide range of plants. As more growers began using it, one piece of feedback appeared consistently: “Can it be made even stronger?” The Tomato System – Storm Edition is the result. Rather than simply reinforcing the original design, I went back to the drawing board and rethought how the entire structure is assembled. The goal was simple: create a version that is noticeably more rigid, more stable, and better suited for demanding outdoor conditions while maintaining the flexibility that made the original system so popular. A Stronger Approach The biggest change is found in the way the system is assembled. Unlike the original Tomato System, which used push-fit vertical posts and external locking clips, the Storm Edition uses threaded vertical posts that screw directly into each support level. This creates a much stronger mechanical connection between sections and significantly increases the overall rigidity of the structure. The threaded design also introduces a unique advantage. New levels can be added without loosening or affecting the sections below. As your plant grows throughout the season, the support structure can grow with it—one level at a time. Cleaner Assembly, Fewer Parts Because each level is securely connected using threaded posts, the side locking clips used by the original design are no longer necessary. The result is a cleaner appearance, fewer loose components, and a more streamlined assembly process. Simply connect the sections using the supplied posts and continue building upward as needed. Designed Around Plant Growth Every plant grows differently, which is why the Storm Edition includes two lengths of vertical posts. Long posts allow for larger spacing between support levels, while short posts can be used when additional support is needed around fruit-heavy branches or dense growth. By mixing the two lengths, you can fine-tune the structure to suit the shape and growth pattern of your individual plant. Built for the Outdoors For gardeners growing directly in soil, the Storm Edition includes optional Soil Anchors. These pointed attachments screw onto the bottom of the vertical posts and help the structure penetrate the ground more easily. They also provide a more secure footing in loose soil, improving stability and helping the system remain firmly planted even in challenging weather conditions. The “Storm Edition” name wasn’t chosen by accident. Not Just for Garden Beds One of the most requested additions was support for existing potted plants. To solve this, the Storm Edition includes an optional Flat Base accessory that allows the system to be used on patios, balconies, greenhouses, windowsills, and other flat surfaces. Simply place the pot inside the base and build the support structure around it. This makes the system just as useful for container gardening as it is for traditional garden beds. The Next Evolution The original Tomato System remains available and continues to be a fantastic option for many growers. https://makerworld.com/en/models/938466-the-tomato-system#profileId-903723 However, if you’re looking for the strongest, most versatile, and most refined version of the concept, the Storm Edition represents the next step in its evolution: Stronger connections. Greater stability. More flexibility. Better support for growing plants. And just like the original, it’s designed to be easy to print, easy to expand, and built to grow alongside your harvest. 🍅 Happy growing!

description: Organize your workspace with this compact, cascading 4-tier pencil and crayon box! Designed with both aesthetics and ergonomics in mind, this cantilever-style box holds up to 48 pencils (12 per tray) and expands smoothly to give you a perfect overview of your color palette. ✨ Update: 10.07.2026: Now with Lid!!! I've added three new files: Lid.stl - It fits snugly with a bit of friction, but it still includes magnet slots so you can combine friction and magnetic forces together. Lid_Brace.stl - You can now secure the closed case with two braces, making this box travel-ready. It currently only works with the 4-level case – if you need other sizes, let me know! Outer_Tray_65.stl - This version of the tray has a 65-degree opening angle (compared to the standard 45 degrees). This makes the levels extend less to the back and stack more vertically, which significantly improves overall stability. All other files are fully compatible. ✨ Key Features: Smart "Eject" Buttons: No more struggling to pick up a pencil. Each slot features a clever built-in button – simply press it, and the pencil pops up for effortless grabbing. Ergonomic Tilt: The bottom tray is equipped with retractable legs. When deployed, the entire organizer tilts toward you. This not only makes reaching for colors easier but also naturally aligns the pencils with the eject buttons using gravity. 100% 3D Printable / No Hardware Required: The entire folding mechanism can be assembled using a custom 3D-printed strap/pin insert that holds everything together perfectly. (Note: Standard M3 screws can be used as an optional alternative). Customizable Magnetic Closure: The trays feature hidden slots for 4x2mm round magnets. Each corner has room for up to 3 magnets. You can use just 1 magnet per corner (as I did in my build) or add more to adjust and fine-tune the exact magnetic pull and snapping force you want when closing the box. ⚙ Printing & Materials: Orientation: All parts are already oriented correctly in the files – just slice and print! Filament: I printed the entire box in PETG, which I highly recommend. You can use PLA for the main trays and body, but the custom strap/pin inserts must be printed in PETG (or ABS/ASA). PLA is too brittle for the mechanical stress of the hinges and may snap. Magnets: 4x2mm round (up to 12 per tray depending on desired strength). 🧩 Printed Parts List & STL Filenames To build the complete 48-pencil organizer (4 tiers), you will need to print the following parts: Part Name Qty STL Filename Notes & Material Inner Tray 4 Inner_Tray_x4.stl Main insert, holds 12 pencils. Outer Tray 4 Outer_Tray_x4.stl Outer shell for each tier. Eject Buttons 48 Eject_Button_x48.stl The lifting mechanism. Frame 4 Frame_x4.stl Aesthetic top trim. Short Link 4 Short_Link_x4.stl Cantilever expansion arms. Long Link 4 Long_Link_x4.stl Cantilever expansion arms. Rear Tilt Legs 1 Rear_Tilt_Legs_x1.stl Deploys for ergonomic tilt. Hinge Strap 8 Hinge_Strap_PETG_x8.stl Print in PETG! 3D printed alternative to M3 screws. you can replace each strap with three M3 screws. 🛠 Additional Hardware Required (Non-Printed) Button Pivot Axis: 4 pieces of standard 1.75mm filament . Cut these to the length of the tray. They serve as a simple, cheap, and effective hinge axis for the eject buttons. Magnets (Optional): 4x2mm round neodymium magnets. The trays feature top and bottom magnet slots in each corner. You can use 1 to 3 magnets per corner depending on how strong you want the snapping force to be. Middle Trays (x2): 8 to 24 magnets per tray (requires both top and bottom slots). Bottom Tray: 4 to 12 magnets (requires top slots only). Top Tray: 4 to 12 magnets (requires bottom slots only). 💡 Pro Tip: I recommend installing top magnets in the top tray as well! A dedicated top cover/lid for easy transport is on my TODO list and will be released in a future update. Linkage Assembly (Choose Option A or B): Option A (100% 3D Printed): Use the 8x printed hinge straps (Hinge_Strap_PETG_x8.stl). Option B (Hardware): Use 24x short M3 screws (6 per tier). 🛠 Assembly Instructions Step 1: Assembling the Inner Trays 1. Gather parts: You need 1 Inner Tray, 12 Eject Buttons, and ~20cm of 1.75mm filament. 2. Position buttons: Place the tray flat and put the 12 buttons into their slots. 3. Thread filament: Push the filament through the side hole, passing through all button hinges. Tip: Cut the filament tip at an angle for easier routing. Twist it if it gets stuck. 4. Trim excess: Cut the filament flush with the outside of the tray. Repeat this entire process 4 times. Step 2: Assembling the Bottom Outer Tray (Tier 1) 1. Attach Links: Counting the side pins from the front: Leave the 1st pinempty, attach a Short Link to the 2nd pin, and a Long Link to the 3rd pin. 2. Attach Legs: Snap the 2 Rear Tilt Legs into the connection points at the back of the tray. 3. Insert Magnets: Place magnets into the top pockets. (Optional: Use a tiny drop of glue to secure them). 4. Attach Frame & Hardware: Snap the Frame onto the top. Secure the links and legs with 6x M3 screws or 2x printed Hinge Straps. Step 3: Stacking and Connecting (Tiers 2, 3, & 4) 1. Add Magnets: Insert magnets into both top and bottom pockets of the new tray. ⚠ CRITICAL: Double-check magnet polarity so the trays attract each other! 2. Shift Linkage: Attach the tray to the tier below. The links shift forward by one slot: The link from the 2nd slot below goes to the 1st slot here. The link from the 3rd slot below goes to the 2nd slot here. 3. Add New Links: • Tier 2: Add a Long Link in the 3rd slot. • Tier 3: Add a Short Link in the 3rd slot. • Tier 4 (Top): Leave the 3rd slot empty. Note: Do not install rear legs on these tiers. 4. Secure: Lock each tier with a Frame and your chosen hardware (screws or printed straps). Step 4: Final Assembly 1. Insert Inner Trays: Press your completed Inner Trays down into the assembled Outer Trays. They are designed for a snug friction fit. 2. Check Direction: Make sure the Eject Buttons are facing the front of the box! 3. Done! Load up your 48 pencils or crayons, extend the rear legs, and enjoy your new cascading organizer. 🚀 To-Do / Future Ideas (V2.0) While I am incredibly happy with how this design turned out and believe it is fully ready to organize your desk right now, a maker's work is never truly done! Here are a few ideas I am exploring for future updates: Dedicated Top Lid: Designing a snap-on cover (utilizing those top magnets) to protect the pencils from dust and make the entire box completely portable. Design Simplification: Exploring ways to merge the inner and outer trays into a single printable piece to reduce both print time and assembly steps. Enhanced Stability: Fine-tuning the cantilever linkage geometry to slightly reduce the backward offset of the expanded tiers, making the fully opened box even more balanced and stable. If you have any feedback or ideas after printing, let me know in the comments!

description: 🍷 FrosNest – Keep your wine cool, enjoy the moment. 🍷☀️ FrosNest is a wine-serving accessory designed to keep your bottles at their ideal serving temperature for as long as possible during meals, aperitifs, barbecues, and summer gatherings. Compatible with the vast majority of 750 ml wine bottles , FrosNest accommodates a standard ice pack, ice cubes, or a combination of both. Its insulated cooling compartment helps reduce heat exchange while its design promotes the circulation of cool air around the bottle. The sections surrounding the bottle that do not contain a cooling source feature a double-wall construction , creating an insulating air gap that slows heat transfer and improves temperature retention. Designed as a complete wine-serving station, FrosNest also includes a dedicated corkscrew holder and an ergonomic carrying handle, making it easy to transport everything with one hand. 🔄 Update – FrosNest V4 Both V2 and V3 remain fully functional and continue to do exactly what they were designed for: helping keep your bottle at its ideal serving temperature for longer. V4 is not a fix , but rather a natural evolution of the concept, making it even more practical and versatile. What's New in V4 🗑️ The mini trash bin is now fully integrated into the FrosNest. There's no longer a separate accessory to print or store. It's always within reach for the cork, foil capsule, Champagne wire cage, or any small waste, helping keep your table clean and organized. 🧊 The cooling compartment has been enlarged to 104 × 40 mm , making it compatible with a wider variety of commercially available ice packs. 🍾 The corkscrew holder has been redesigned to better accommodate a larger range of waiter's corkscrews while making insertion and removal easier. 🥂 A new optional removable wine glass holder is now available for both V3 and V4. It is compatible with many stemmed wine glasses featuring a stem diameter of less than approximately 9 mm . Up to two holders can be mounted on each side , allowing you to carry up to four wine glasses together with the FrosNest. I hope this new evolution makes FrosNest even more enjoyable to use while preserving everything that made the previous versions so successful. 🍷❄️ 🔄 Update – FrosNest V3 Thanks to your amazing feedback, FrosNest has already evolved! 😊 First of all, the original version remains fully functional and already does exactly what it was designed to do: help keep your bottle at its ideal serving temperature for longer. However, after reading your suggestions and feedback, I wanted to push the concept even further. FrosNest V3 builds upon the original design by improving the circulation of cooled air around the bottle while keeping the same simple, practical, and efficient philosophy. V3 introduces several improvements: ❄️ The cooling compartment has been moved above the bottle. Since cooled air is denser than warm air, this new position promotes a more natural circulation of cool air around the bottle, helping to maintain its serving temperature even more effectively. 🍾 The bottle opening has been increased to 90 mm , making FrosNest compatible with most standard Champagne bottles in addition to regular 750 ml wine bottles. 🎨 The FrosNest logo has been reduced in size , minimizing filament color changes on multi-material printers and reducing filament waste during color swaps. 🗑️ A new optional accessory has been added: a removable mini trash bin , perfect for holding the cork, foil capsule, wire hood, or any small waste that would otherwise end up on the table. This project is a parametric decorative Bubble Tray. Fully programmed in OpenSCAD, it features an elegant border made entirely of perfect spheres. The design utilizes a flawless vertical transition between the base and the spheres, eliminating any empty gaps or flat triangles at the absolute bottom (Z=0), ensuring an impeccable fusion finish. --- UNLIMITED CUSTOMIZATION --- The mathematical model automatically scales and calculates the entire distribution of spheres along the perimeter, ensuring accurate tangency and spacing regardless of the chosen length, width, or sphere radius. With support for 1 to 6 layers of stacked spheres, the combinations are virtually endless. --- PARAMETER GUIDE --- 1. Main Dimensions - Tray Length and Width: Defines the overall size of the round shape. - Base Thickness: Controls the height of the solid internal bottom plate. 2. Sphere Geometry (Advanced Settings) - Sphere Radius: Defines the diameter of the spheres and, consequently, the thickness of the outer wall. Change this to achieve anything from delicate small spheres to massive giant spheres. The model recalculates the required quantity automatically. - Height Ratio: Adjusts the height of the containment border relative to the sphere radius. - Overlap Factor (Penetration): Controls how much the spheres intersect each other laterally. The default (0.20) provides the optimal visual balance and structural strength. 3. Sphere Layers (Towering) - Number of Layers: Create anything from a simple flat tray (1 layer) to a deep basket-style tower with up to 10 perfectly stacked layers. - Vertical Overlap Factor: Controls the mathematical fusion between upper and lower layers (recommended: 0.40). 4. Customization and Details - Bottom Logo: A dedicated space to deboss your brand/logo on the smooth bottom face. --- TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS & PRINTING --- - Clean Print Bed: Unlike other beaded models, this project's base is mathematically flat with no angular cuts on the spheres touching the build plate. - Support-Free Design: The sphere geometries are calculated to guarantee a progressive overhang angle easily handled by modern printers. No internal or external supports are required! - Premium Finish Tip: For a truly professional, textured clay or ceramic look, enable the "Fuzzy Skin" feature on the Outside walls only in your slicer! --- RECOMMENDED PRINT SETTINGS (Bambu Studio / OrcaSlicer) --- - Layer Height: 0.16mm (Optimal for the vertical curves of the spheres) - Wall Generator: Arachne (Recommended for filling small fusions) - Infill: 10% Gyroid or Cross Hatch - Supports: No supports needed! - Fuzzy Skin (Optional for premium finish): Contour, Thickness: 0.3mm, Point distance: 0.8mm 💡 Pro Tip: Enable Variable/Adaptive Layer Height in your slicer.

Description This model let's you make your own custom bookfinity books inside Bambu Studio. Just select a book size, change the text, and upload an image to make your custom book to store your stuff. This version is with the Latch to lock the book. If you want it without the latch and use just magnets, use this version here . What is Bookfinity? Bookfinity is a storage system that let's you store gridfinity stuff inside custom book shelf toolboxes. These look fantastic on a bookshelf and let's you grab your tools and components with ease. It's the most organised storage solution for any hobby. It consists of two parts: a bottom part which holds the part, and a top cover that includes the hinge. These two parts are aligned with the tabs and need superglue to attach together (Assembly Instructions below). How to use this Easy Edit Model? Step 1 - Select your book thickness Find the book size you want to edit. The 3MF files are organized by the bin height, eg 3U Books take 3U bins. Each profile has the following sizes: 2x2, 2x3, 3x3, 3x4, 3x5, 4x4, 4x5. Step 2 - Select your book Select your book size, and rotate the screen so you're looking underneath like this: Step 3 - Change to Objects On the left hand side, change the Process from Global to Objects. Step 4 - Click on your book Click on the book on the build bed, you'll see the text options on the left hand side. Step 5 - Select Edit Text Right click the main text and press “Edit Text”. A popup will appear Step 6 - Change the text Change the input text and you can change the size and move it around. (You can change the font too, but certain fonts don't print too well). Step 7a - Create an SVG (optional) There are many free SVGs online, and I've uploaded all of the SVGs I've used on Bookfinity on this model. If you need a custom one, you can use ChatGPT with the following prompt: “Create an image of an svg-style stencil with thick black lines of: ” and insert the name of the tool. Step 7b - Convert the PNG to SVG (optional) If you create a PNG, you'll need to convert it to an SVG. You can do it with a free site like FreeConvert. Step 8 - Insert the SVG Right click your book, press “Add Modifier” > “SVG”. TIP: if you insert your SVG, and it's just a rectangle this is because the SVG has an outline / border. This is wrong and won't work. If you generated the SVG using FreeConvert or similar, try change one of the options. on FreeConvert, I found if you go to Advanced Settings and change the "Color Mode" to “Black & White” and redownload it, it fixes this issue. Step 9 - Move, Scale and Rotate your SVG Using the Move, Scale and Rotate buttons, get your SVG where you need it. Step 10 - Set the depth of the SVG Firstly find your SVG on the menu on the left (remember to press “Objects” if you've gone off it). Right click it and press “Edit SVG”. A popup will appear. On the popup, set the Depth to 0.60mm and ensure the “From Surface” distance is 0.00mm. You can use “Use Surface” but it makes it invisible on the prepare tab so harder to use. Step 11 - Set the colour of your SVG On the left hand side, right click the SVG, press “Change Filament” and select the colour you wish to use, eg Black. Step 12: Enable Prime Tower Change Process back to "Global", then under the “Others” tab, find “Prime Tower” and select “Enable”. Move the prime tower so it doesn't clash with your model. This will make the books print much cleaner. Step 13 - Boost the model How to assemble a book Add superglue to the glue area shown below 2. Install the Bolts Install the latch using an M3 x 30mm Bolt, and an M3 Nyloc to the top cover. The nut should be at the top of the book. Install an M3 x 30mm bolt with an M3 Nyloc nut to the bottom cover. 3. Print a Gridfinity holder for your tool / stuff. If you're just looking for storage bins, these Simple Bins are guaranteed to fit. 4. Add Magnets (optional) Insert 4x D4 x 2mm magnets into the cover and base to make the books stay closed. These are available on the Bambu Shop, linked below. Notice a mistake? Got advice / requests? Please leave comments, or DM me (: Remember to also post photos of your books! Posting Remixes Yes! Upload your custom books as remixes for other people to help them out, get inspo and earn yourself some points! Use of AI Some of the SVGs used on the book covers were made using AI. The 3D model was made by human. The cover photo was made on PowerPoint, but an AI background remover tool was used. All other photos are real. Update (25/06/2026) The 7U and 8U versions are currently working progress. Please be patient these take a while to create in Bambu Studio and I'm on Holiday until Mid July.

description: ✨ Parametric Desk Sign – Create Your Own Personalized Version Transform any name, word, or phrase into a modern 3D printed desk sign. This fully parametric design allows you to create personalized signs while keeping the same clean style and proportions. Adjust your text, size, and thickness to create a perfect display piece for your desk, gaming setup, office, bedroom, events, or as a custom gift. ⭐ Key Features ⚙️ Fully Parametric Design The model automatically adapts to your custom text while maintaining balanced proportions and a strong structure. ✏️ Personalized Text Create your own: Names Gamer tags Room signs Event displays Custom messages Gifts 📏 Adjustable Size & Thickness Scale the sign to fit your space while keeping the design stable and visually balanced. 🖨️ 3MF Ready – Optimized for 3D Printing Prepared for easy printing with clean geometry and maker-friendly setup. 🎨 Color Customization Choose your own filament colors: Two-color swaps Contrasting text and base Premium silk PLA finishes 🚫 Support-Free Printing Designed for clean FDM printing without supports. 🧠 Design Details This is not just a simple text model. The parametric system rebuilds the sign based on your input: Text spacing is adjusted automatically Base length adapts to the text Structure stays balanced Geometry remains clean for printing Each personalized sign becomes a unique version of the design. 📏Here is a quick breakdown of all the parameters in the script, organized by their categories: 1. Global Settings Scale_factor : Multiplies the overall size of the entire model (e.g., 2 makes it twice as big). Center_Z_axis : If true, floats the model in mid-air (useful for viewing). Keep false for 3D printing so it sits flat on the bed. 2. Font Selection Selected_Font : Chooses the font style for your text. 3. Bold Settings Bold_Text : Turns on/off a thickening effect for the text. Bold_thickness : Controls how much extra thickness is added when Bold is turned on. 4. Main Text Settings Your_name : The actual word, name, or phrase you want to display. Font_size : The 2D visual size of the main text. Text_height : The 3D physical thickness (height) of the main text letters. 5. Backplate Settings Back_height : The 3D thickness of the solid base that holds the sign together. Border_size : Adds an extra solid outline/padding around the main text on the backplate. 6. Underline Options Show_underline : Toggles a decorative line underneath the main text. Underline_thickness : How thick the underline bar is. Underline_Gap : The empty vertical space between the bottom of the letters and the underline. Underline_extension : How far the underline sticks out past the left and right edges of the text. 7. Background Text Options Show_background_text : Toggles a large background letter or word (like a watermark behind the main text). Bg_text : The specific letter or word for the background (e.g., the first letter of a name). Bg_size : The visual size of the background text (usually much larger than the main text). Big_letter_height : The 3D thickness of the background text. Set to 0 to make it flat against the backplate. Bg_xy_space : Adds a thick outline/padding around the background text to make it chunkier. Bg_x_offset / Bg_y_offset : Moves the background text left/right and up/down to position it perfectly behind the main text. 8. Color Options Back_color : Sets the color for the base/backplate, the border, and the large background letter. Text_color : Sets the color for the main text and the underline. 🖨️ Print Settings Recommended: Layer height: 0.20 mm / 0.16 mm quality Walls: 2–3 Infill: 10–20% Supports: Not required Great results with color swaps to highlight the raised lettering. ❤️ Share Your Makes I love seeing what people create! description: Schluss mit Schmutz am Poolboden! Wer einen Bestway Lay-Z-Spa besitzt, kennt das Problem: Sand, kleine Blätter und Schmutz sammeln sich unweigerlich am Boden, und die integrierte Pumpe schafft es nicht, diesen gezielt zu entfernen. Dieses funktionale Modul löst das Problem elegant und einfach. Es verwandelt die Standard-Ansaugdüse deines Pools in einen effektiven Bodensauger. Anwendung: Ein Filterbällchen in das Modul einlegen (ich verwende die von Steinbach). Den Gartenschlauch an den 1-Zoll-Anschluss anstecken. Die Poolpumpe (Filterfunktion) einschalten. Das Modul auf die Ansaugdüse stecken (der Unterdruck fixiert es sofort). Den Poolboden mit dem Schlauch absaugen. Die Story hinter dem Design – Vom "Fail" zum Feature! Eigentlich war der Plan ein ganz anderer: Ich wollte den Adapter ursprünglich mit einem passenden Gewinde versehen, um ihn fest auf die Düse aufzuschrauben. Da es aber verdammt schwer war, die exakten Spezifikationen des Pool-Gewindes zu finden (und ich beim Abmessen wohl auch ein wenig zu doof war...), passte das gedruckte Gewinde hinten und vorne nicht. Kurz geärgert, kurz nachgedacht – und festgestellt: It’s not a bug, it’s a feature! Das mühsame Auf- und Abschrauben im Wasser bei jedem Reinigungszyklus wäre viel zu umständlich gewesen. Die neue, gewindelose Version wird jetzt einfach nur noch über den Einlass geschoben. Durch den Unterdruck der Pumpe saugt sich das Modul bombenfest an und lässt sich nach der Reinigung sekundenschnell wieder abnehmen. Schneller und einfacher geht es nicht! Geniales Plug & Play: Das Modul wird bei laufender Pumpe einfach auf die Ansaugdüse im Pool gesteckt. Der Unterdruck der Pumpe saugt das Teil fest an und hält es sicher in Position – ganz ohne Schrauben oder Klemmen. Integrierter Schmutzfang: Im Inneren des Adapters ist exakt Platz für ein handelsübliches Filterbällchen (z. B. von Steinbach). Dieses fängt den aufgesaugten Schmutz direkt auf, bevor er überhaupt in die Pumpe oder den Hauptfilter gelangen kann. Das Filterbällchen kann danach einfach ausgewaschen werden. Universeller Anschluss: Das Modul verfügt über einen 1-Zoll-Anschluss. Hier kann ein Standard-Gartenschlauch (z. B. mit Gardena-Kupplung) aufgesteckt werden. Mit dem freien Ende des Schlauchs kannst du nun bequem den gesamten Poolboden absaugen. description: I wanted to make a simple enrichment toy that would keep my cats entertained for a little longer without needing batteries or anything complicated. The Kibble Egg is designed to be filled with dry kibble or small treats. As your cat or small pet bats it around, it rolls across the floor, randomly dispensing pieces through the four 12mm openings. Because the treats come out gradually, it encourages play while making your pet work a little for their food. It's a fun way to add a bit of enrichment to mealtimes, help slow down enthusiastic eaters, and encourage natural hunting and foraging behaviour. It also works well for other small pets that enjoy chasing treats. The 12mm dispensing holes are ideal for small kibble, although the amount released will vary depending on the size and shape of the food you use. I designed this for my own cats and it's been great watching them chase it around the room, never quite knowing where the next piece of kibble will appear. I hope your pets enjoy it too!

Perfect for both personal use and the production of unique, exclusive pieces. --- CUSTOMIZATION --- The model is designed so that any user can configure it quickly, with the number of hearts being automatically calculated to fill the entire perimeter! 1. Basic Settings - Tray Length & Width: Maximum exterior dimensions of the tray (mm). - Base Thickness: Thickness of the base along the Z-axis. - Cut Inner Hearts: Enables boolean subtraction to remove the inner portion of the hearts, yielding a smooth interior wall. - Alternating Layers: Enables horizontal offset (half-step) on even layers, aligning geometry in a brick pattern. - Number of Layers: Quantity of heart rings stacked along the Z-axis. - Heart Base Size: Size of the heart (mm). The script recalculates the perimeter and automatically adjusts the instance count. 2. Engraving & Text Settings - Enable Top Text: Adds embossed (raised) text to the center of the base's top face. - Enable Bottom Logo: Adds debossed (engraved) text to the base's bottom face. 3. Advanced Settings For users who want fine-grained control over mesh and placement: - Heart Width / Thickness / Height Ratio: Individual scale of the heart on its local X, Y, and Z axes. - Heart Size Multiplier: Global scale (XYZ) applied to the heart. - Heart Facing Rotation: Angular rotation (local Z-axis) of each heart at its origin. - Heart Z Offset: Z-axis displacement of the heart layers. Negative values intersect with Z=0 (cut plane), generating a flat bed adhesion area. - Heart Radial Offset: Radial displacement of the anchor line. Negative values increase volumetric intersection with the base. - Lateral and Vertical Overlap Factor: Interpenetration rate between adjacent instances. --- TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS & PRINTING --- - Clean Printing Base: The parametric bottom is cut perfectly flat on the Z-axis, ensuring maximum bed adhesion without the fragility of the heart tips. - Support-Free: The design ensures progressive overhangs without the need for any supports in FDM printing. - Premium Finish Tip: For a wonderful textured ceramic look, enable the "Fuzzy Skin" option on the outer contour in your slicer! How to use Fill it partly with water, leave enough empty space for ice expansion, freeze it, and use it as a flat cooling block. The slim rounded shape makes it easy to place inside a cooler bag, lunch bag, backpack pocket, or near small DIY cooling setups where a flatter ice pack is more convenient than a bulky block. This design uses a recessed filling area and a separate cap, helping keep the overall shape compact and easy to handle. The ice pack uses an internal honeycomb-style structure to help divide the water volume into smaller sections and support the flat walls during freezing. This helps reduce deformation and stress from ice expansion while keeping the model slim and lightweight. Important Do not fill completely. Water expands when frozen. Always leave empty space inside before freezing. The internal structure does not mean the model can be filled completely. It only helps support the shape and divide the water volume. This is a 3D printed container, so always test for leaks before using it near electronics, food, bags, or temperature-sensitive items. Leak / material preparation note Possible leaks are not automatically caused by the model design. This is a functional 3D printed container, so water-tightness depends heavily on the material, printer condition, slicer settings, and calibration. Before using the ice pack, make sure your filament is properly dried, especially PETG, and that your printer is calibrated for that exact material. Incorrect flow, too high or too low temperature, poor layer bonding, wet filament, under-extrusion, weak walls, dirty nozzle, or modified print settings can all cause leaks. For better sealing, print slowly, use enough walls and top/bottom layers, check extrusion and flow calibration, and make sure the cap and filling area are printed cleanly. description: A modular picture frame system that fits any canvas size. Print the corners and connectors once, then generate custom rail segments to match your artwork dimensions. Canvas clips lock the artwork in place from the back without glue. A small drop of CA glue on the connector pins is recommended for a permanent frame joint. Works with canvas depth of 10mm or more. Four plate types included in default print profile Corners are fixed parts that connect the frame at 90 degrees. Each corner takes up 65mm on each side it connects to. Print 4 for any frame. Connectors are the printed pins that join rails to corners. Print one connector per part, corners and rails combined. For example, 4 corners and 6 rails need 10 connectors total. Canvas clips are retaining pins that hold the artwork securely in the frame recess from the back. Each corner has 2 clip holes and each rail has 1. Print one clip per hole for maximum hold. Note: one hole on the top rail is reserved for wall hanging. Frame rails are the straight segments generated to your dimensions. Two generators are included Frame Side Generator calculates the rail length from your canvas size, Single Frame Rail Generator lets you enter an exact length for replacement parts or custom segments. How to use Frame Side Generator Enter your canvas side length in mm. Minimum 170mm. Enter the number of rail segments for that side. Aim for at least 40mm per segment, otherwise the connector pins won't fit. The generator calculates the segment length: (canvas length - 130) / number of segments. Click a generated part in the preview to confirm its exact length before printing. Repeat for the other side if your frame is not square. How to use Single Frame Rail Generator Enter the exact rail length you need. Minimum 40mm. Use this for replacement parts or when you already know the dimensions. Material notes PLA works well for most sizes. For larger frames (above approximately 400mm per side) consider PETG or a stronger material for better rigidity. Assembly Apply a small drop of CA glue to each connector pin before pressing into the corner sockets and rail ends. Slide the rails and corners together and let the glue set. Place your canvas in the recess and insert the canvas clips to lock it in place. If you print it, please leave a rating - it helps a lot.
