Airsoft Impact Spring Grenade The performance of the grenade is heavily linked to the springs, I wouldn't go higher than 50mm for the AEG spring (I used a stock one) because I see no real benefit for it. As for the trapezoidal (mid cap) springs, the best quality you can find, the better. I used the springs from a Cyma mid cap 140bb mag but I believe Maple Leaf sells a "better" spring kit for mid-caps for around 15€ so if you are going to invest, you may want to consider in that possibility. If you end up using the Maple Leaf ones or any possible better springs, please do let me know. As for the 4mm pen springs, as long as it's around 4mm in diameter and compresses enough for the traps to compress and let the BBs through, it should be good. Hardware needed: - 1 AEG Spring (or similar) cut to 40-50mm (length will depend on your spring strengh) - 1 Mid-cap (140bbs) or 1 trapezoidal spring cut to 6 sections of 90mm - 2 4mm pen springs cut to 6 sections of 4-5mm (don't use the ends, it might not compress enough= - 13 M2x8 bolts (M2x6 can also work but I'd rather use the x8) - 1 1.5mm allen key to be used as a pin or anything you want to use instead I've given 0.3mm tolerance overall between parts but sanding might be needed for optimal performance. You want the BB to go through smoothly and every part to slide well. All that while not having a huge play between parts either. The skin (printed in TPU) is optional but highly recommended for durability, knowing this is something you'll be throwing around. If something is to break in the interior, it's more likely to be the piston shaft due to the middle section thickness, so this is one of the reasons why I wouldn't over do the spring length, more length means more power but it also means more stress, and in this case, more power wouldn't give you better results. The skin also serves an aesthetic purpose, so I'd like to have more variety in the future. description: OpenPrintSense - 3D Printed BLE Flex Sensor Glove OpenPrintSense is an open-source project that combines 3D printing, hardware, and software to create a wearable finger tracking system. The key innovation is a fully 3D-printed flex sensor that uses conductive TPU filament - as the sensor bends, its electrical resistance changes, allowing precise measurement of finger flexion. Data is transmitted wirelessly via BLE to an Android smartphone. How It Works: The 3D-printed sensor combines flexible TPU with conductive filament. When you bend your finger: The conductive filament stretches This increases the electrical resistance The microcontroller reads the resistance change via analog input The bend angle is calculated and sent to the app Use Cases: 🎮 Gesture-based game controllers 🤖 Robot hand control 🏥 Rehabilitation therapy tracking 🎵 Musical instrument interfaces 📊 Motion capture for research Electronics: Microcontroller: Seeed XIAO nRF52840 Sense Power: USB-C or 3.7V LiPo battery Wires: For connecting sensor to microcontroller 3D Printing Materials: Flexible Base: Bambu Lab TPU 90A - Flexible structure Conductive Element: Recreus FilaFlex Conductive - Variable resistance sensing Read the GitHub for more information on assembly and functionality: https://github.com/PaBu04/OpenPrintSense

model_name: Wind Turbine Project | Functional Simple Turbine
description: This is a heavily modified and fully functional remix of the excellent "Basic Wind Turbine" by kjt270000 . This remix transforms the original core concept into a practical, power-generating system designed specifically for apartment balconies and off-grid experimentation. This project includes completely redesigned mounting hardware, weatherproofing additions, structural reinforcements, and a complete perfboard electronics enclosure to harness the wind and charge an 18650 lithium-ion battery. 🛠️ What's New in this Remix? Two Optimized Sizes Medium Version: Retains the 24mm motor from the original model. Ideal for standard winds and smaller spaces. Large Version: Upgraded to house a 32mm motor, significantly increasing power generation potential for easier battery charging. Balcony-Ready Mounting System The mounting system has been completely engineered from scratch to easily clamp onto a typical balcony barrier. The Mast: Designed to use a standard 32mm (external diameter) PVC pipe with a 2.5mm wall thickness as the main tower. Free Rotation Yaw: To ensure the turbine can freely track wind direction (yaw) without friction, the design incorporates a standard bearing (27mm External Diameter / 15.5mm Internal Diameter) at the pivot point. Structural & Weatherproofing Upgrades Motor Cover: Added a top cover for the motor housing to improve weather resistance. (Note: While it provides splash and light rain protection, leaving the turbine out in heavy, continuous rain is still not encouraged). Tail Support: A new stabilizing brace was added to the tail section. This prevents the tail from sagging or bending under its own weight over time due to the natural layer orientation of FDM printing. Smart Cable Management On both versions, the main pivot body features a specific internal routing path. The cables run straight from the motor, inside the PVC pipe, and out the bottom. This prevents the wires from wrapping around the mast as the turbine rotates. ⚡ Electronics Overview (No Custom PCB Required!) Hardware Components List Core Modules & Power 1x 18650 Lithium-Ion Battery (3.7V, unprotected cell is fine since the circuit has protection) 1x 18650 Single Cell Battery Holder 1x TP4056 Lithium Battery Charging Module (Ensure you get the version with the built-in protection circuit—it has OUT+ and OUT- pads in addition to B+ and B-). 2x MT3608 DC-DC Step-Up Boost Converter Modules (Often marked as HW-045). Basic Electronic Components 4x Rectifier Diodes (1N4007 are standard, but 1N5819 Schottky diodes are highly recommended here for better efficiency and lower voltage drop). 1x Electrolytic Capacitor (Values around 470µF to 1000µF, rated for at least 16V or 25V). 1x Perfboard / Prototype PCB (Standard dot-matrix board, cut to fit your 3D printed enclosure). Miscellaneous Hookup wire (22-24 AWG stranded wire is ideal for flexibility) Solder How It Works (The Circuit Logic) Input & Rectification: The wind turbine motor generates erratic, fluctuating voltage (and possibly AC depending on the motor). The four diodes act as a Bridge Rectifier , ensuring the electricity flows in the right direction regardless of which way the wind spins the turbine. The Capacitor smooths out this rippling voltage. Boosting to Charge: The turbine might not always generate the 5V needed to charge the battery. The first MT3608 boost converter takes the smoothed voltage and steps it up to a steady 5V. Battery Management: The 5V feeds into the TP4056 module , which safely charges the 18650 battery and protects it from over-charging and over-discharging. Output Power: The 18650 battery outputs around 3.7V. The second MT3608 boost converter takes this battery voltage and steps it up to a stable 5V (or 12V, depending on what you are trying to power with the turbine). Step-by-Step Assembly Guide Important Pre-step: Before soldering the MT3608 modules into the final circuit, connect a temporary power source to their inputs, hook a multimeter to their outputs, and turn the little brass screw on the blue potentiometer until they output exactly your desired voltages (e.g., 5V for the first one). Step 1: The Rectifier Circuit (Power Input) Solder the 4 diodes onto the perfboard in a bridge rectifier configuration. Connect the two wires coming from your wind turbine motor to the AC input sides of the diode bridge. Solder the electrolytic capacitor across the positive and negative outputs of the diode bridge. Note: Capacitors have polarity; ensure the negative stripe side connects to the negative trace. Step 2: Voltage Stabilization (First Boost Converter) Connect the Positive output of the capacitor to the VIN+ on the first MT3608 module. Connect the Negative output of the capacitor to the VIN- on the first MT3608 module. Tune this module to output exactly 5V. Step 3: The Charging Circuit Connect the VOUT+ of the first MT3608 to the IN+ (or standard positive input pad) of the TP4056 module. Connect the VOUT- of the first MT3608 to the IN- of the TP4056 module. Solder the positive (red) wire from the 18650 battery holder to the B+ pad on the TP4056. Solder the negative (black) wire from the battery holder to the B- pad on the TP4056. Step 4: Output Power (Second Boost Converter) Connect the OUT+ pad from the TP4056 to the VIN+ pad of the second MT3608 module. Connect the OUT- pad from the TP4056 to the VIN- pad of the second MT3608 module. Adjust the potentiometer on this second MT3608 to your final desired output voltage (e.g., 5V for charging a phone, 12V for LED strips). Solder your final output wires to the VOUT+ and VOUT- pads of the second MT3608. Enjoy building, and may the wind be in your favor!

NEMA 17 High-Torque 2-Stage Planetary Gearbox (1:25 Ratio) This is a compact and robust 2-stage planetary gearbox specifically designed for NEMA 17 stepper motors . With a total reduction ratio of 1:25 , it provides a significant torque boost for your robotics projects, actuators, or DIY automation. The design is optimized for 3D printing, featuring easy-to-identify parts and a straightforward assembly process. Technical Specifications: Total Gear Ratio: 1:25 Motor Compatibility: NEMA 17 Stepper Motor Bearings: 8x (10x5x4mm) Fasteners: M3x30mm screws & M3 Heat-set inserts Reduction Mechanism: Dual-stage planetary gears Bill of Materials (BOM): To complete this build, you will need: Bearings: 8 pieces of 10x5x4mm (standard MR105 or similar). Screws: 4x M3x30mm bolts. Inserts: 4x M3 heat-set inserts (to be installed in the motor mount housing). Key Design Features: Error-Proof Assembly: To prevent confusion during assembly, the Stage 1 Ring Gear is narrower than the Stage 2 Ring Gear. Always use the thinner ring for the first stage (closer to the motor). Secure Mounting: All stages are held together by M3x30mm screws that thread directly into heat-set inserts melted into the motor mount for maximum durability. Assembly Instructions: Preparation: Press the M3 heat-set inserts into the dedicated holes on the Motor Mount . Stage 1: Press-fit the Stage 1 Sun Gear onto the NEMA 17 motor shaft. Install the Narrower Ring Gear onto the motor mount. Place the Stage 1 Planet Carrier (with bearings and planet gears installed). Stage 2: The Stage 2 Sun Gear should be mounted onto the Output Shaft (which connects the two stages). Install the Wider Ring Gear for Stage 2. Place the Stage 2 Planet Carrier. Final Step: Place the Top Cover Plate and secure the entire assembly using the four M3x30mm screws . Tighten them evenly into the inserts in the motor mount. My Educational Mechanical Examples Series This model is one of my educational mechanical mechanism examples on 80mm x 80mm base plates. You can find all models of the series in this collection => [Mechanical Mechanism Examples] The present model This is an educational model of self-centering chuck. Brief Description A self-centering chuck is a device often used with a lathe . A lathe is a machine tool that rotates a workpiece and presses a cutting tool against it to remove material, producing shapes that are symmetric about the axis of rotation. During turning, a workpiece often has to be re-clamped from a different side, and each time this is done the rotational center of the workpiece must be made to coincide exactly with the rotational center of the lathe. A self-centering chuck moves several jaws — arranged symmetrically around the lathe's axis — inward or outward together without breaking that symmetry, continuously varying the radius of the circle traced by their gripping faces. Because the jaws remain symmetric, a rotationally symmetric workpiece held in a self-centering chuck settles naturally with its own axis aligned to the lathe's axis, requiring no fine adjustment. The self-centering chuck shown here has three jaws, whose positions are set by a ring into which an Archimedean spiral is cut. An Archimedean spiral is a spiral whose adjacent turns are spaced a constant distance apart. When the ring turns at a constant rate, the point where the spiral crosses a given radius travels along that radius at a constant speed. The underside of each jaw carries a straight rack that meshes with this spiral, so as the ring turns and the crossing point moves, the jaw — whose motion is constrained to the radial direction — is carried along the radius by that motion. On the plane through the middle of a jaw, the mechanism is this simple, but the finite width of the rack teeth makes the story a little more complex. As the figure below shows, each rack tooth has to curve to follow the spiral. The curvature of an Archimedean spiral is not constant — it is tighter on the inside and gentler on the outside — so as a jaw travels along the radius, the curvature of the spiral tooth it meshes with changes as well. To keep the rack teeth from interfering at any position the jaw can reach, each tooth is shaped for the worst case: its inner edge is cut to the largest radius of curvature that occurs over the tooth's range of travel, and its outer edge to the smallest. This makes the valley between teeth wide and deep enough everywhere to clear the spiral ridge without interference. To keep all three jaws at the same distance from the center, the rack on each jaw is offset in phase by one third of a tooth pitch, as shown in the figure above. Only when the jaws are fitted in the correct order do the three jaws sit at equal distances from the center. In the photograph above, each jaw is stepped, growing thicker toward the center, as the left figure below. A jaw of this kind is called an inside-diameter (ID) step jaw. It is designed for two modes of use: gripping a workpiece placed between the three jaws by closing the jaws onto its outer surface, and supporting a hollow workpiece from within, by inserting the raised central step into the bore and opening the jaws against the inside of the hole. Both modes were demonstrated in the youtube video above. The model also includes, as optional parts, an outside-diameter (OD) step jaw, which instead grows thicker toward the outside (central figure), and a flat jaw with no steps (right figure). The OD step jaw is used to hold a workpiece whose diameter is too large to be gripped by the central part of the jaws. A working chuck on a lathe hides all of its mechanical detail inside a steel body; here, laid open, the spiral and the racks show plainly how symmetry is turned into motion. Related model In the model of Groove Cam , the follower motion was limited along an arc by the swinging arm. In the present model, the teeth on the bottom surface of the jaws can be regarded as followers running in the Archimedean spiral groove. There, the followers' motion is limited along straight lines by the linear guide, instead of arcs. The model of Archimedean spiral gear, included in "Educational Gear Examples 2" shows a combination of Archimedean spiral with a pinion gear, instead of rack. Case This model is compatible with the case included in my first set . Printing Use the models named ???-printable.stl for printing . The models named ???-assembled.stl are provided just to show how they should be assembled. Use well-dried PETG to have better dimensional accuracy. Use 0.1 mm or 0.08 mm layer height to have smoother surfaces. Use slow printing speed for overhangs. Select “Random” seam position to have smoother rotation. Randomly distributed seam should be easily worn out after some wearing.Printing Sanding and Filing Note that, in this model, the rotation of the bases for bearings is intentionally made not too smooth. Sometimes, the gears suffer from the stringing effect and/or elephant foot effect, resulting in a too tight fit to the shafts (they are designed with a 0.15 mm radial clearance). If you see rough surface on the shafts due to stringing, sand off the roughness with a small piece of sand paper. If you feel the gears do not rotate smoothly due to an elephant effect, widen the hole slightly by using a thin round bar file. Without those issues, the parts should rotate very smoothly with minimal friction. Assembly Place the knob on the shaft and secure it with the retaining ring. Place the ring gear. Push the legs of the linear guide into the holes on the base plate. They will snap into place. While turning the ring gear counter-clockwise, slide the jaws into the linear guides one by one to make them mate with the spiral, referring to the number of dimples on the jaws. The one with single dimple should be the first, one with two dimples the second, and one with three dimples the last. Since three jaws have their teeth at different phases, if they are placed with wrong order, they will not be at same distance from the center. The order of insertion is what matters — any jaw can go into any guide, as long as the single-, double-, and triple-dimple jaws are inserted in that order. To replace the jaws to those of different type, turn the ring gear clockwise fully until the jaws come out from the linear guide. Then slide the replacing jaws in following the step 4. Find them in this collection: https://makerworld.com/collections/15048577-my-educational-mechanism-models Happy printing! description: 5-Speed Manual Gearbox with Reverse This is a fully functional, highly detailed 5-speed manual transmission model (plus Reverse) designed for educational demonstration, engineering enthusiasts, or anyone who loves mechanical design. Every major internal component of a real manual transmission is represented here, including the input shaft, counter shaft, main output shaft, synchronizer hubs, synchronizer rings, sliding sleeves, and a reverse idler gear. Are you looking for a great weekend activity to keep your kids entertained for hours? This project perfectly combines 3D printing technology with classic hands-on crafting. Anyone who has tried letting kids paint a standard 3D printed model (made of PLA or PETG) with watercolours or tempera knows it’s a struggle – the paint slides off the plastic surface, runs, and doesn't cover well. Plaster casts made from these TPU molds are a complete game-changer. Plaster has the perfect absorbency, so colors stick flawlessly, dry instantly, and look incredibly vibrant. You only need to print these flexible molds once, and you can cast plaster dinosaurs for your kids every single weekend, over and over again. 💡 Why TPU 95A? These molds are designed specifically for printing with TPU 95A flexible filament. Thanks to the unique compliance of this material, you don't have to worry about complex mold-release draft angles during modeling. The model is designed with an optimal wall thickness of 1.5 mm , which provides the perfect balance: the mold keeps its geometry perfectly and doesn't bulge under the weight of liquid plaster, yet it remains flexible enough that you can incredibly easily peel it off the hardened cast like a banana skin. No getting stuck, no broken details. 🛠️ Recommended Print Settings: Material: TPU 95A (e.g., Bambu TPU). Wall Thickness / Perimeters: 3 walls (crucial for maintaining the mold's stability). Infill: 10%. Note: Print directly from the rear spool holder of your printer, do NOT use the AMS , as flexible materials tend to get tangled and stuck in it! For a perfectly smooth inner surface, make sure your TPU is well dried before printing. 🧪 Step-by-Step Casting Guide for Kids: Preparation: Place the clean and dry TPU mold on a flat, stable surface. Pro Trick for Zero Bubbles: Lightly spray the inside of the mold with a spray bottle filled with water and a single drop of regular dish soap. The soap acts as a wetting agent – it lowers surface tension, allowing the plaster to flow flawlessly into the smallest details without leaving air bubbles on the surface. Alternatively, you can use a release agent made of wax dissolved in alcohol. Mixing the Plaster: Mix standard white hobby plaster with water according to the package instructions. Make sure to mix the consistency a bit thinner (like runny pancake batter) – this is very important to ensure the plaster flows easily and without resistance into all the fine details and crevices of the dinosaur. Pouring: Carefully pour the plaster into the mold. It is recommended to leave about 2–3 mm from the top rim for easier handling. Once poured, gently tap the mold against the table a couple of times (vibration) to release any remaining trapped air bubbles to the surface. Releasing the Mold: Wait about 20 to 30 minutes. Once the plaster is solid and warm to the touch (due to the exothermic reaction), gently peel the TPU mold away by bending it. Thanks to the 1.5 mm thin wall, it will come off effortlessly. Creative Finale: Let the cast dry completely (ideally in the sun or on a radiator until it turns bright white and "rings" when tapped). Then, just give your kids brushes, tempera, or acrylic paints and let them create!

A minimalist hand-driven planetarium that turns the six classical planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn — at astronomically accurate relative speeds. 10 cm wide, 5 cm tall. A desk piece that models the solar system (as it was known in the 1700s!). Why only 6 planets? I came across a gear train for a planetarium that was designed by Scottish astronomer James Ferguson in the mid-1700s. At the time, Uranus and Neptune had not been discovered. His design used a single stacked gear to drive 6 planets, and I thought it was cool! In order to print it however, I had to include a dedicated connector gear for Jupiter-Saturn, as the teeth would have been too small to be printed. Description of the model can be found page 300 here . Parts Required Requires 7 ball bearings with these diameters: Sun = 12 mm Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars = 6 mm Jupiter, Saturn = 8 mm I included spheres for printing, but I think marbles or ball bearings would look much better. Kinetic Galton Board A kinetic Galton board that demonstrates the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution instead of the usual Gaussian you get from a classic bead-and-peg Galton board. It went semi-viral on Instagram (4M+ views), so I'm publishing the files here for anyone who wants to build one. Watch it run: https://www.instagram.com/p/DZauWk2SiXA/ How it works There are two chambers, left and right. The left chamber holds about 400 balls resting on a slider above a fast-spinning cylinder fitted with two fins. The fins agitate the balls and inject energy into the system. The balls collide with each other and with the chamber walls, behaving like gas particles in a box. At the top-right corner of the left chamber there is a small hole, roughly one ball wide. A ball only escapes (effuses) through this hole when it arrives with the right velocity. On the right side there are about 14 bins. The bin dividers are slightly shorter than the height of the escape hole, so a ball that effuses has to fall a small distance before reaching the tops of the bins. The physics is the interesting part: Because the hole is about the size of a single ball, a ball leaving it has essentially no vertical velocity at the moment of escape. So the time it takes to fall the small gap to the bins is the same for every ball . With d = v·t and t constant, the horizontal distance a ball travels (and therefore the bin it lands in) is proportional to its speed at the moment of effusion . Read the bin, and you've effectively measured how fast that ball was moving when it escaped. Do this for all ~400 balls, which have been colliding and exchanging energy like gas molecules, and the bins fill in to trace out the signature Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution . Printing There are two versions depending on what motor you have. Version for CIM (FRC) I built mine around an FRC CIM motor , just because I had some lying around. They're big and frankly overkill for this, but a lot of FRC people have them on hand. If that's you, open the Version for CIM folder and print the STL files there. Version for 775 For everyone else, the most common suitable motor is a 775 . They're cheap and easy to get almost anywhere. Open the Version for 775 folder and print the parts there. Both folders also include the raw STEP files if you want to modify anything. Cover The cover on mine is laser-cut acrylic . If you don't have a laser cutter, there's an STL so you can print it instead out of a transparent material, it just won't be as clear as acrylic. If you want to chase clarity, look up guides on printing crystal-clear PETG, though I didn't have much luck with it myself. Balls You need about 400–600 balls . They are 4 mm diameter , so do not substitute airsoft BBs, those don't work. To save you from duplicating a ball 400 times in your slicer, there's a 20×20 grid of them included. A few notes: Add a brim when printing the grid, otherwise the balls pop off the build plate. The sliced result should look like this: After printing you'll have a sheet with all the balls attached to it. Don't try to pull them off by hand , you'll tear the sheet and it becomes a miserable job getting the sheet off the balls. Instead, use pliers and twist each ball off the sheet. It's tedious, but it works. 400 balls took me about 20 minutes. Assembly and operation You will need 1x 775 motor, 2x M4x8 bolts, 4x M3x8 bolts Assembly is straightforward Place the balls into the device. Insert the slider. Shake the balls into the left chamber. Important: Use the slider to drop the balls onto the agitator while it is already spinning . If the balls surround a stationary agitator and you try to spin it up, it will stall the motor and the whole thing jams. That's it, spin it up and watch the distribution build.

description: This Rubber Band Powered Helicopter is a simple, fully 3D-printed flying model with no tail boom, no gears, no electronics, and no extra hardware. Just two contra-rotating rotors and a rubber band between them—that is the whole idea. Wind the rotors, store energy in the band, and let go. The top and bottom rotors spin in opposite directions, canceling torque so the body stays stable without a tail rotor. Lift comes from the combined action of both rotors working together. The design is intentionally minimal. Print the parts, add one rubber band, and you are ready to fly. No screws, bearings, motors, or purchased kit parts are required. ------------ A rubber band runs directly between the upper and lower rotors. There are no gears—the band connects the two rotors and does all the work. When you wind the model, the band twists and stores elastic energy. On release, the band unwinds and drives both rotors at the same time—but in opposite directions. Because the rotors turn against each other, their reaction torques cancel out. That is why this helicopter does not need a tail boom or tail rotor. The contra-rotating setup does the job in a clean, compact way. Everything you need is printed in plastic except the rubber band. The fuselage holds the two rotors in alignment and gives you something to grip while winding. ------------- - A 3D printer and filament - One rubber band - One drop of glue That is it. No other parts to buy or hunt for. --------------------- I printed mine on a Bambu Lab A1 mini using PLA. Keep prints light where you can; less weight means better lift from the same rubber band. Use a drop of glue to secure the hook to the upper rotor from the top.

description: Overview This is a fully 3D printed wheel and chassis system for a trap powered car — a classic physics and engineering project. The design was built for a 4th grade science fair project to investigate how wheel size and tire material affect how far a trap-powered car travels. Three experiments were run per configuration (18 total runs), covering three wheel sizes and two tire materials. The winning combination — large 200mm wheels with TPU rubber tires — averaged 49.1 meters (161 feet) on a single spring release! The car is powered by a standard snap-style rat trap, which stores energy in its spring and releases it through a string wound around the rear drive axle. This design intentionally uses a rat trap rather than a mouse trap — the larger spring arm and stronger spring store significantly more energy, which is why the car travels so far. Build Levels — Start Simple, Go Further This design has three levels of complexity. Print only what you need. Level Plates What You Get 1 — Build the Car Plate 1 only A complete, working trap powered car with small wheels. Great standalone toy or first project. 2 — Wheel Size Experiment Plates 1 + 2 and/or 3 Swap in medium or large rear wheels and measure how far the car travels with each. One variable, easy to test, clear results. 3 — Tire Material Experiment All 4 plates Add TPU rubber tires and compare plastic wheels versus rubber tires. Requires a direct drive printer for TPU. The full science fair setup. Most people only need Plate 1. Print more plates if you want to experiment. How It Works The car converts stored spring energy into motion. When the trap arm releases, it pulls a string wound around the rear drive axle, spinning the wheels and launching the car forward. As the car moves, elastic potential energy from the spring converts to kinetic energy (motion). Wheel size and tire material both matter: Larger wheels cover more distance per rotation and roll over small surface irregularities more easily Rubber (TPU) tires grip the surface better, transferring more energy into forward motion instead of losing it to wheel slip Printed Parts Structural Parts — print in PLA or PETG Part Qty 3MF File Notes Body 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 One mounts to each end of the spring trap Arm 1 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 Extends the trap arm for more string travel Arm Cap 1 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 Secures the arm extension to the trap arm Axle 4 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 2 hubs per axle × front + rear axle (fits 1/4" bamboo dowel) Wheel Small (100mm) 4 Complete-Kit — Plate 1 2 front (fixed) + 2 rear (small config) Wheel Medium (150mm) 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 2 Print Plate 2 twice for a pair Wheel Large (200mm) 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 3 Print Plate 3 twice for a pair Everything is in one 3MF file with 4 plates. Plate 1 includes 4 small wheels: 2 for the front axle (always small) and 2 for the rear axle (small-wheel configuration). For medium or large rear wheels, print Plate 2 or Plate 3 twice — front small wheels are already on Plate 1. Tire Treads — print in TPU 95A Part Qty 3MF File Notes Tire Small 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 4 See tire plate note below Tire Medium 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 4 See tire plate note below Tire Large 2 Complete-Kit — Plate 4 See tire plate note below Tires are optional — the car works with plastic wheels only (we tested both!). TPU tires make a big difference though — see the results table below. Tire plate note: Plate 4 uses TPU 95A with supports enabled — filament and supports are already configured in the 3MF. All three tire sizes are arranged concentrically on the plate — the rings nest inside each other because the smaller tires fit through the center hole of the larger ones. To get a matching pair, print Plate 4 twice. To print only one size, delete the other two objects in Bambu Studio before slicing. Non-Printed Materials 1× Rat trap — Victor M205-9 Wide Plastic Pedal (recommended) or equivalent large rat trap. Use a rat trap, not a mouse trap — the stronger spring is essential for distance. 2× Bamboo dowel, 1/4" diameter, ~17.5" long (front axle + rear drive axle). 12" may also work. Dowels vary in straightness and diameter — pick the straightest ones, especially for the axles. If a dowel fits loosely, a small drop of glue holds it. If too tight, try another from the pack. Fishing line (monofilament) — light and strong 1 small metal staple Print Settings Structural Parts (PLA or PETG) Layer height: 0.2mm Walls: 3 Infill: 15% (gyroid or grid) Supports: None required Bed: Textured PEI plate PLA is recommended for most users — it's easier to print and more than strong enough for this application. PETG was used in the original build and also works great. TPU 95A Tires Layer height: 0.2mm Walls: 3 Infill: 15% Print speed: 30–40 mm/s (slow down for TPU reliability) Supports: Enabled (pre-configured in the 3MF for Plate 4) Direct drive extruder required — disable AMS/multi-material system for TPU Assembly Instructions Mount the trap to the body — slide the snap trap into the body's mounting slots Install axles — push bamboo dowels through the front and rear axle holders on the body Attach wheels — press wheels onto the ends of the rear axle Press-fit tires — stretch TPU tires over each wheel rim gradually, working around the rim evenly. Take your time — forcing one side too quickly can crack the wheel. Install arm extension — attach the printed arm to the trap's spring arm using the arm cap Attach string — tie one end of fishing line to the tip of the arm extension. Press a staple into the center of the rear axle and bend one prong out as a small hook. Tie a loop at the other end of the string and hook it onto the staple. When the trap arm releases, it pulls the string until the loop slips off the staple — this clean release is what launches the car. How to Launch Set the trap arm back (use caution — keep fingers clear of the snap mechanism) Wind the string around the center of the rear axle (consistent winding keeps the car straight) Place the car on a smooth, flat surface behind your start line Release the trap arm — the car launches! Tip: Wind the string at the axle center every time. Off-center winding causes the car to veer left or right, reducing distance. String length matters: when fully wound, the loop should slip off the staple just as the trap arm reaches its resting position. Too short and it releases before full energy is transferred; too long and the string tangles in the axle after release. Running It as an Experiment This design was built for a science fair, and it works great as a controlled experiment. Here's how to set one up: 1. State your hypothesis Make a prediction before you test. For example: "I think larger wheels will make the car go farther because each rotation covers more distance." 2. Identify your variables Independent variable (what you change): wheel size, or tire material Dependent variable (what you measure): distance traveled, or time rolling Constants (what stays the same): launch surface, string winding, number of winds, who releases the arm 3. Run multiple trials Do at least 3 runs per configuration and record each individually. Use the average — single runs vary too much to be reliable. 4. Record your data Wheel Size Tire Material Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 Average Small 100mm Plastic Small 100mm Rubber (TPU) Medium 150mm Plastic Medium 150mm Rubber (TPU) Large 200mm Plastic Large 200mm Rubber (TPU) 5. Analyze and conclude Compare your averages. Did the results match your hypothesis? What surprised you? Consider what other variables might have affected your results (surface texture, string length, dowel straightness). Notes & Tips The car can travel a surprisingly long distance — 49 meters is half a football field! Make sure you have plenty of room Surface quality matters — bumps, cracks, and slope all affect results Rubber bands can be used instead of TPU tires as a quick alternative for traction Front wheels are small fixed wheels and don't need to change between experiments Bamboo dowels vary from pack to pack — test a few and use the straightest ones. Axle fit affects both alignment and roll distance.

A few printing notes: Silk filaments look really cool, but I recommend not using them for the nut or connector. If you do, print a test part of the connector and nut first. Assembly: The assembly is pretty straightforward. To begin, create a ring of 4 triangles of alternating colors. Then attach an alternating-colored triangle to each of the open nodes. Finally, link them together. It's not difficult, but there are a lot of them. Tips: Make sure the parts are inline when the gear teeth are meshed. Hold the connector and not the triangle when locking the nut, or you may cause it to slip a gear tooth. Best Surface for Maximum Effect The surface you spin the rattleback on matters a lot! To get the best reverse-spin effect, use a hard, smooth surface like glass, hard plastic or wood. description: I've printed the SMARS tracked rover to see if I can adapt to use an ESP32-WROVER-CAM Dev.B microcontroller which has a built-in 2Mpx camera so I can turn it into a tracked mobile, WiFi controlled webcam. Although the ESP32-WROVER-CAM has enough GPIOs to use with the L298N dual motor driver, when the webcam is turned on in the sketch along with the WiFi, there are only 4 usable GPIOs remaining. Luckily, I found that it should be possible to use just the 4 GPIOs to control the two motors, but it also requires that the L298N EN-A and EN-B pins be raised to +5V. If you discarded the two jumpers that usually come with the L298N, then use two DuPont wires to connect the two enable pins on the driver to +5V. The print profile available for the BambuLab A1 Mini worked perfectly although I cannot use the IR sensor mount since the chassis is fully occupied by the L298N and the 2S1P 18650 pack with switch and voltmeter, but more importantly, there are no more GPIOs left to use the IR sensor. As you can see from the photo I took of the result is not very good looking but it does move quite nicely. I have two 100rpm DC motors which give it a decent scurry speed. The code I can share upon request if anyone wants to give it a go. Ping me and I can share the sketch and describe the wiring since it took a bit of experimenting to get the ESP32 to eventually be able to control the two motors as desired.

A simple educational electromagnetic motor powered by a battery, copper coil, and magnet. Perfect for learning the basics of electricity, magnetism, and motor mechanics. Designed as an easy beginner electronics project with a clean 3D printed base. How to Build: This simple electromagnetic motor works by using a battery, a copper wire coil, and a permanent magnet to create rotational movement. First, bend two paper clips so they can hold the coil while still allowing it to spin freely. Attach the paper clips to the battery or the 3D-printed holder using electrical tape, making sure they are stable and properly aligned. Next, create a coil by winding insulated copper wire into a circular shape with around 6–10 turns, leaving two wire ends sticking out on each side. Carefully remove the insulation from the wire ends: only strip the insolation from one site this is impotent if done on both it wont function. This allows the electric current to switch on and off during rotation, which keeps the motor spinning. Place the coil into the paper clip supports so it can rotate with minimal friction. Then position a permanent magnet directly underneath the coil. Once the battery is connected, give the coil a small push with your finger. The magnetic field generated by the current inside the coil interacts with the permanent magnet, causing the coil to continuously rotate and creating a simple electric motor. model_name: My Social Battery — “how charged do I feel?”
description: My Social Battery — a tactile “how charged do I feel?” slider for kids Slide the lightning bolt and click through five stages — from flat-battery exhausted to fully charged — to show, at a glance, how much social/emotional energy you’ve got left. It’s a friendly, fidget-satisfying self-regulation and communication aid shaped like an AA battery. Built for kids 4–11 , and great for SEND / AAC / visual-support classrooms and calm corners — but honestly it’s for anyone who’s ever run out of “people battery.” Why you’ll like it A proper click. A print-tuned ratchet gives a crisp tick between stages and a firmer “settle” at each of the five homes — and it clicks exactly the same force in both directions (a symmetric twin-arm spring, not a one-sided one). Chunky lightning-bolt handle — rounded and wide, sized to survive a five-year-old, easy for little fingers to grab. Five emoji faces on removable colour panels: 😵 exhausted → 🙁 low → 😐 okay → 🙂 good → 😀 fully charged. Swap the panels toollessly — they snap in and pop out, so you can re-theme it (a 6-panel feelings set is on the way). Wall-mount or hand-hold — two rear keyholes or a Command-Strip on the flat back. Print settings Material: PLA. Stiff/standard PLA gives the crispest click (the spring is tuned for it). Nozzle / layers: 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layers. ~15 % infill is plenty. Supports: Tree supports for the Body only (they release much more cleanly than normal supports). Everything else prints support-free. Orientation (as exported): Part Orientation Supports Body front face up tree supports (for the channel roof / pockets) Slider flat (as exported) none — the spring must print flat so it flexes in-plane Grip (bolt) flat, bolt-face on the bed none Back cover flat none Panels ×5 flat none Two-colour panels: print each panel in its stage colour and swap to black at the face layer (Z ≈ 2.0 mm) so the embossed emoji prints black. On an AMS this is automatic; otherwise it’s a single manual filament change. Colours (suggested): Panel 1 red · 2 orange · 3 yellow · 4 light green · 5 dark green; body white/grey; bolt gold/yellow. Assembly (a couple of minutes, one drop of glue) The grip is a separate part because it’s far too wide to thread through the front slot. Drop the Slider into the body channel from the back — the square post pokes out through the front slot. From the front, press the Grip onto the post ( a drop of super-glue = a permanent, kid-proof bond). Press the Back cover into its rebate from behind until the sprung tabs snap home (firm tug to service later). Snap the five Panels into the front pockets (pop them out later via the sloped pry-notch at the bottom edge). Mount: two rear keyholes (slide onto screws) or a Command-Strip on the flat back. Notes Wall-mount screws: the keyholes suit M3.5 screws — pop the screws into the wall first and slide the plaque down. Little parts: there are no loose small parts once assembled (the grip is glued; panels are captive snap-fits).

真实月球自转周期与绕地公转周期完全同步（27.3天），因此永远以同一面朝向地球。本设备不设月球自转轴，公转时月面固定指向地心，精准复刻真实天体状态。 2. 专业轨道、天体倾角与模型物理参数 2.1 核心夹角参数 黄赤交角（地轴倾角） ：23.5°，固定不变。是四季、极昼极夜、昼夜长短变化的根本原因。 黄白交角 ：黄道面（地球公转轨道面）与白道面（月球公转轨道面）的夹角为 5°09′ 。本设备通过倾斜的月球公转副臂（或轨道支撑结构）机械实现该夹角，与月球是否具备自转轴无关。 月球自转轴倾角（约1.5°）因设备无月球自转，不涉及演示。 2.2 两大轨道平面 黄道面 ：地球公转轨道平面。 白道面 ：月球公转轨道平面，与黄道面成5°09′。 2.3 模型实物尺寸与间距（桌面适配差异化缩放） 部件 直径 / 间距 太阳模型 36 mm 地球模型 80 mm 月球模型 21 mm 地日中心距 200 mm 地月中心距 120 mm 缩放说明 ： 真实日地直径比约109:1，距离比约11700:1。若在桌面模型上同时保真直径与距离比例，模型将庞大到无法用于教学。因此本设备采用科学差异化缩放： 太阳模型取较小直径（36mm）以避免遮挡光源并保证光照均匀性； 地球模型适当放大（80mm）以便清晰展示表面标注（赤道、回归线、极圈等）； 地轴倾角、黄白交角、光照几何、公转与自转相对运动关系均严格保真 ，所有天文现象的演示原理（四季、极昼极夜、月相、日月食）完全不受影响。 ✅ 该缩放方式属于专业天文教学模型的常规设计，并非科学错误。 3. 整机部件详细说明 部件名称 功能说明 太阳光源模型 模拟平行太阳光，恒定发光。光源规格及供电方式可自行适配。 地球模型（带固定地轴） 内置23.5°固定倾角地轴，表面标注赤道、回归线、极圈。支持自转及公转。 月球模型（潮汐锁定） 无自转，公转时固定面指向地心，沿白道面绕地运行。 地轴岁差旋进调节旋钮 用于初始校准地轴指向或演示岁差。 常规演示中应保持锁定 ，不得用于模拟四季更替。 地球公转主臂 带动地球沿黄道面绕日公转，配合刻度底座显示节气位置。 月球公转副臂 带动月球沿白道面绕地公转， 内置5°09′黄白交角结构 。 刻度底座 标注黄道轨道、二分二至点、四季位置，辅助定位。 电源开关 控制太阳光源启停，可按需适配。 4. 首次操作与天文基准手动归位 本设备为纯手动模型，无自动运行功能。所有位置调节均需人工操作。 基准归位目的 ：设定统一的初始状态，确保后续演示符合天文原理。 手动归位步骤 （纯人工对位）： 将地球公转主臂转至底座 春分刻度 位置。 调节地轴岁差旋进轴，使地轴指向与底座上的“北极指向标记”对齐（若无标记，可设定地轴倾斜方向垂直于日地连线，且北极指向远离太阳的一侧——此为春分标准指向）。 锁定地轴岁差旋进轴 ，后续演示中不再转动。 将月球公转臂转至 朔点（日地之间） 基准位置。 目视检查黄道面、白道面倾角无偏移，完成归位。 核心原则 ：除岁差演示或初始校准外，地轴指向一旦设定，在整个公转演示中必须保持固定。四季、极昼极夜等现象完全由地球公转自动产生，无需手动改变地轴朝向。 5. 基础天体运动演示操作 5.1 昼夜交替与晨昏线 开启光源，匀速转动 地球自转轴 （自西向东）。 面向光源为 昼半球 ，背向为 夜半球 ，明暗交界线为 晨昏圈 。 顺着自转方向，由夜入昼为 晨线 ，由昼入夜为 昏线 。 可观察：晨昏线始终与太阳光线垂直，赤道全年昼夜等长。固定地球转角可展示同一时刻全球昼夜分布。 5.2 太阳直射点周年移动 保持地轴指向固定 （已锁定岁差旋进轴），缓慢转动 地球公转主臂 。 公转过程中，由于地轴倾角固定，太阳直射点会在南北回归线之间移动： 夏至（公转至夏至刻度）直射北回归线 冬至直射南回归线 春分/秋分直射赤道 5.3 四季更替演示（正确方法） 前提 ：地轴指向已锁定，不再调节。 按顺序公转至四个节气刻度，观察光照情况： 节气 公转位置 太阳直射点 北半球季节 南半球季节 春分 春分点 赤道 春季 秋季 夏至 夏至点 北回归线 夏季 冬季 秋分 秋分点 赤道 秋季 春季 冬至 冬至点 南回归线 冬季 夏季 注意 ：演示时 不要 转动地轴岁差旋进旋钮，否则会错误地认为四季需要手动调节地轴指向。 5.4 全球昼夜长短差异 在公转不同位置，观察不同纬度的昼夜长度： 夏至 ：北半球昼长夜短，北极圈极昼；南半球相反。 冬至 ：北半球昼短夜长，北极圈极夜；南半球相反。 春分/秋分 ：全球昼夜平分。 5.5 地球五带划分 通过光照范围与直射点移动，演示热带（南北回归线间）、温带（回归线至极圈）、寒带（极圈以内）的划分。 6. 进阶专业天文现象演示（极昼/极夜） 正确演示前提 ：地轴指向固定（已锁定岁差旋进轴），仅通过公转改变地球在轨道上的位置。 6.1 夏至日北极极昼、南极极夜 开启光源，公转主臂转至 夏至刻度 。 保持地轴指向不变（春分时设定的指向），此时地轴北极自然倾向太阳。 观察晨昏线与北极圈相切，北极圈内全为白昼（极昼），南极圈内全为黑夜（极夜）。 转动地球自转轴，极昼/极夜区域不改变。 6.2 冬至日南极极昼、北极极夜 公转主臂转至 冬至刻度 。 地轴指向仍为初始设定，此时地轴南极倾向太阳。 晨昏线与南极圈相切，南极圈内极昼，北极圈内极夜。 6.3 春分、秋分无极昼极夜 公转至春分或秋分刻度，太阳直射赤道，晨昏线过两极，全球昼夜等长，无极昼极夜。 6.4 极昼极夜范围渐变演示 缓慢连续转动公转主臂，观察极昼/极夜范围从极点逐步扩大至极圈，再逐步缩小的动态过程，完整还原全年变化。 7. 月相、日食、月食完整演示（结合黄白交角） 7.1 月相周期演示 开启光源，手动转动 月球公转轴 ，月球沿白道面公转。观察月球被照亮部分的形状变化： 新月（朔）→娥眉月→上弦月→盈凸月→满月（望）→亏凸月→下弦月→残月→新月。 （因潮汐锁定，月球同一面始终朝向地球，但被照亮区域随公转位置变化。） 7.2 日食演示（朔日限定） 将月球转至 日—地之间（朔点） ，并微调月球公转角度以抵消黄白交角偏差，使日、月、地三者近似共线。此时月球影子落在地球上，可演示日全食/日偏食效果。 解释 ：因黄白交角存在，多数朔日不共线，故日食罕见。 7.3 月食演示（望日限定） 将月球转至 日—地延长线（望点） ，微调角度使日、地、月共线，地球阴影覆盖月球，演示月食。同理，并非每望日都发生。 8. 标准操作注意事项 四轴结构精密，转动需轻柔匀速，禁止暴力操作。 常规演示中地轴岁差旋进轴应保持锁定 ，仅当演示岁差或初始校准时方可调节。 演示晨昏线、极昼极夜、日月食时，建议在暗光环境下进行。 可根据需要自主适配光源亮度与供电方式。 设备为精密模型，禁止摔落、撞击、浸泡；儿童操作需成人陪同。 禁止私自拆卸轴体，以免四轴联动精度失效。 9. 常见故障与原理答疑 Q1：为什么月球不会自转？是否为缺陷？ A：不是缺陷。真实月球为潮汐锁定，自转与公转周期相同，永远同一面朝地。本设备科学还原该特性。 Q2：为什么演示四季时不需要转动地轴岁差旋进旋钮？ A：真实地球公转中，地轴在空间中的指向保持恒定（指向北极星附近）。四季更替完全由公转位置改变太阳直射点而产生。若在公转中手动旋转地轴，将得到错误原理。本设备的地轴岁差旋进轴仅用于初始校准或演示岁差。 Q3：为什么太阳模型比地球小？ A：这是为了桌面教学的可行性而进行的工程缩放。真实比例无法在桌面模型中实现，本设备牺牲尺寸比例但保留了所有角度、光照几何和相对运动关系，不影响任何天文现象的教学。 Q4：黄白交角5°09′是如何实现的？月球没有自转轴会影响吗？ A：黄白交角是月球公转轨道面（白道面）与地球公转轨道面（黄道面）的夹角，通过倾斜的月球公转副臂机械实现，与月球是否自转无关。本设备正确保留该夹角，用于演示日月食发生条件。 Q5：为什么无法每次朔望日都演示日月食？ A：设备精准还原了5°09′黄白交角，多数朔望日三者不共线，与现实一致，非故障。 Q6：极昼极夜、晨昏线演示效果不明显怎么办？ A：检查公转位置是否准确对应节气刻度，并确认地轴指向已锁定且倾角无误（未误触岁差旋钮）。重新按第4章归位即可。 Q7：晨昏线为什么不会和经线完全重合？ A：仅春分、秋分两天太阳直射赤道，晨昏线与经线重合；其余时间因地轴倾角，晨昏线与经线存在夹角，本设备可完整呈现该变化。

description: Descubriendo a Pitágoras – Demostración práctica interactiva ¿Cómo demostrar visualmente que la suma de los cuadrados de los catetos es igual al cuadrado de la hipotenusa? Este proyecto convierte el famoso Teorema de Pitágoras en una actividad manipulativa que permite comprenderlo de forma intuitiva y práctica. Las piezas almacenadas en los dos cuadrados de los catetos pueden extraerse y reorganizarse para rellenar completamente el cuadrado de la hipotenusa, demostrando físicamente la relación: h² = c² + c² El conjunto se guarda en una práctica caja circular con tapa de rosca, ideal para el aula, actividades educativas, aprendizaje en casa o simplemente para los amantes de las matemáticas y los objetos didácticos impresos en 3D. Perfiles de impresión incluidos Se incluyen dos perfiles para la base de la caja: Standard Quality Boquilla: 0,4 mm Altura de capa: 0,20 mm Tiempo aproximado: 3 h 11 min High Quality Boquilla: 0,4 mm Altura de capa: 0,20 mm Perfil High Quality de Bambu Lab Tiempo aproximado: 4 h 23 min El resto de componentes pueden imprimirse utilizando los perfiles incluidos en las distintas placas. Organización de las placas El proyecto está dividido en cuatro placas para facilitar la impresión: Placa 1: Base de la caja. Placa 2: Tapa de rosca. Placa 3: Piezas de un color. Placa 4: Piezas del segundo color. Esta distribución permite imprimir cada color por separado, evitando cambios de filamento innecesarios y reduciendo considerablemente el tiempo total de impresión. Archivos incluidos Para facilitar la personalización y el uso con sistemas multicolor: Archivos OBJ para los componentes que requieren varios colores, permitiendo colorearlos directamente desde el laminador. Archivos STL para las piezas que se imprimen en un único color. Montaje No requiere soportes ni montaje complejo. Una vez impresas las piezas, basta con colocarlas en sus respectivos compartimentos y comenzar a experimentar con una de las demostraciones matemáticas más conocidas de la historia. Si te gusta este proyecto, considera dejar un like, una valoración o compartir una fotografía de tu impresión. ¡Disfruta descubriendo a Pitágoras!

description: To be honest, I've only played D&D a handful of times. The first time, I joined a campaign that was already in progress, and my character's role ended up being... a loot box (a very important role for the story, of course!). The second time was playing Baldur's Gate 3 on the highest difficulty. We made it all the way to level 4... and then we lost :( Since this contest is all about imagination and role playing, I wanted to create something that felt interactive instead of just decorative. I started looking for drawbridge models, and to my surprise, there weren't many available (especially ones inspired by D&D) so I decided to design one myself. The mechanism is actually quite simple. It uses three pulleys and a hand crank to raise and lower the bridge. Surprisingly, the most challenging was decorating the model and making it look like a proper medieval gate (i mean, i tried). This is both the largest and longest print I've ever made, using close to 500 grams of filament. I tried to reduce material usage as much as possible, especially in the base, which prints with just 5% infill. Thankfully, all of the print plates completed without any issues. The model is optimized to print without an AMS. If you'd like a two color gate/door, you can simply add pause commands during the print to swap filament. For the finishing touches, I added small grilles, and a couple of crocodiles in the water. I also took the opportunity to try some plastic safety eyes I bought on AliExpress, and they really add a lot to the final result. That said, I've also included printable eyes if you prefer a fully printed build. I'm going to try to upload an assembly video (video only, no audio). The assembly process is very straightforward, but I think it could still be helpful. If you're interested in printing the model and have any questions, feel free to ask! Materials ~20 cm of yarn/wool , Used as the rope for the pulley system. I experimented with shoelaces, but they didn't provide enough friction. Glue , For final assembly. A tool for support removal , Most parts print support-free, but the door/gate itself requires a few supports that can be a bit difficult to remove. If possible, printing the supports in PETG can make removal much easier.

Capture Incredible Timelapses With The AllSky Capsule. The AllSky Capsule is a camera system for astrophotography. This version, The AllSky Capsule, is inspired by the Ikea BEGÅVNING Glass Dome . Costing just £13, I couldn't resist the opportunity to try and fit an AllSky system inside. The AllSky Capsule is built around Arducam's LN051 120 Degree Ultra Wide Angle Lens . I Have chosen this lens for several reasons. Firstly, the cost is very good for the quality of the optics; secondly, the image it produces is almost perfectly flat. I didn't want any distortion or fish-eyeing, it is the largest FOV I could find without significant distortion. Lastly, it seems to be widely available. INFO These are magnetic separation racks for 0.2mL PCR sized tubes. Works for SPRI, ConA, or any magnetic beads. My lab is a big fan of the epicypher racks but they cost $500 dollars so we were always fighting over the one, and even then when you have more than 8 or 16 samples it is inconvenient to always switch out tubes while doing high through put experiments. I wanted more racks so I designed these with a similar style and functionality to the epicypher racks with some added improvements. 1.Racks come in 8-tube and 12-tube sizes so you can make full use of the multichannel and scale up easier 2.Magnets are removable, so you can simply slide the magnet out rather than removing the tubes from the rack 3.The magnet can be turned around to work better for either small or large volumes. 4. Less than 1% of the price of Epicypher magnet racks (even with the cost of magnets) BEFORE YOU PRINT While smooth, semi-textured, and textured plates all work, I find that printing on a textured plate results in a tighter fit of the magnet holders inside the rack. I prefer the slightly looser fit I get when printing on my BIQU cool plate. If you use my print profile then you don't need any supports, however, these are kind of tall prints so I recommend making sure you have a clean bed and dried filament to avoid any adhesion errors. If you are having adhesion problems then you can take it a step farther and use a cool plate and/or a brim. ASSEMBLY You will need 10x5x3mm magnets. One 8 tube rack takes 16 magnets and one 12 tube rack takes 24 magnets. After printing, glue the two halves of the magnet holder together with the magnet holes in the same orientation. Then, insert the magnets. While they have a snug press fit, I find that they stay in better if the magnets on either side of the holder have opposite poles facing each other (the orientation where they stick together). A dab of super glue doesn't hurt either.

This high-efficiency mousetrap car is powered purely by the spring mechanical energy of a Windhager mousetrap and utilizes a real gear system to maximize distance. The design runs incredibly smooth and achieved a personal track record of exactly 30 meters! To wind it up, the car must be rotated by three-quarters of a turn at the main gear, featuring a gear ratio of 1 to 64. Required Hardware: 6x 6700 ZZ Ball Bearings (10 x 15 x 4 ) 1x M3 Socket Head Screw 43 mm total length, partially threaded with a 20 mm smooth shank 1x Windhager Mousetrap Step-by-Step Guide: Spring Preparation: Remove the spring from the Windhager mousetrap. Trim the protruding wire ends so that about 2 cm remain, and bend them so they stick out at a 90° angle relative to the spring. Inserting the Spring & Sleeve: Push the printed plastic sleeve inside the spring. Then, insert the spring into the main motor cavity of the chassis with the thicker side of the spring facing inward. Main Gear & Core Screw: Place the large main drive gear onto the spring. Pass the M3 screw through the gear and the spring to lock everything into place. Tighten it enough to eliminate wobbling, but ensure it remains loose enough to spin freely without excessive friction. Gearbox Assembly: Press one ball bearing into each of the middle gears. If the fit is tight, gently tap them in using a hammer. Carefully mount these geared assemblies onto their designated pins on the chassis. Axles & Wheel Bearings: Install the axles along with the remaining bearings onto the frame. Tip: For the wheel axles, you can optionally use 3D-printed bearings. However, for the high-load drivetrain gears (Step 4), real metal ball bearings are strictly required! Attaching the Wheels: Finally, press-fit the wheels onto the axles – the large wheels go in the back, and the small wheels go in the front.

description: This Boxer Air Engine is a modular flat-four style pneumatic engine inspired by the classic boxer layout, where opposing pistons move in opposite directions for smooth, balanced motion. The full assembly is built from 4 separate single-cylinder air engines, and each one can run on its own. This lets you print, build, and test each cylinder module individually before installing them in the shared frame and combining them into the complete boxer engine. Each single-cylinder module is based on my previous single-cylinder engine concept, but with an updated crankshaft design: - Square front shaft - Square rear socket (hole) These features allow the crankshafts to connect end-to-end so all four cylinders can be phased correctly in the final boxer setup. --------------------- I printed mine on a Bambu Lab A1 mini using PLA. I used a little baby oil for lubrication. Some sanding or light filing is to be expected, but usually not very much. All moving parts must move very easily for the engines to work correctly. This engine can run from a balloon, an air duster, or an air compressor. ------------------------------- - Mark each crankshaft and flywheel with a marker before final assembly. - Align timing so Cylinders 1 and 2 are on their power strokes at the same time. - Align Cylinders 3 and 4 the same way with each other, but opposite phase to Cylinders 1 and 2. This staged approach makes troubleshooting easier and helps ensure a smooth-running final engine. ----------------- - Modular design: 4 independent single-cylinder engines combine into one boxer engine. - Each cylinder can be tested individually before full assembly. - Interlocking square crankshaft ends simplify mechanical coupling. - Correct phase alignment is critical for balanced boxer operation. - Marking parts helps maintain timing during final build.

Die Platte 4 enthält einen Ständer mit Fläche für ein Schild (Siehe in der pdf), die Platte 5 ein Ständer ohne Fläche für ein Schild. - nach meiner Farbkodierung ist: weiß die Antriebswelle, schwarz der Abtrieb von Planetenträger, grau das Gehäuse, rot die Zahnräder, grün die Lager und gelb der Stopfen bzw. die Schrauben - ich habe folgendes geklebt: die Stifte in das Gehäuse, den Stopfen in das Gehäuse, die inneren Lager, direkt am Gehäuse - die Deckel können auf das Gehäuse geklebt werden, dann kann das Getriebe jedoch nicht mehr auseinandergenommen werden. Damit das Getriebe trotzdem zusammenhält ist die Klammer da. Diese kann von unten auf das komplette Gehäuse geschoben werden - die Kleinen Lager gehen lassen sich nur sehr schwer in die Zahnräder pressen. Dafür diese vorsichtig mit etwas diese in die Zahnräder schlagen, bis die Lager deutlich unter der Kante des Zahnrades sind - der Deckel vom Planetenträger hat extra eine Aussparung, sodass man ein Zahnrad sieht. Die „Schrauben“, welche Wirklichkeit nur Stifte sind, gingen bei mir sehr schwer. Wenn ihr das Getriebe wieder gut aufmachen können wollt, diese am besten ein wenig kleiner Skalieren und evtl. an den Deckel vom Planetenträger kleben - das angehängte pdf enthält die Beschriftung (52mmx22mm), ich habe dies auf Papier (DIN A4) ausgedruckt, welches man als Aufkleber verwenden kann. Es lässt sich aber auch mit normalem Papier ausdrucken und aufkleben - das ganze Getriebe mit Gestell braucht ca. 130g Filament - ich habe für die Stützen unter dem Gehäuse ein paar Schichten Support for PLA verwendet. Wenn kein Support for PLA Filament vorhanden ist dies einfach zu PETG ändern. Das funktioniert genauso. (Wenn das Getriebe aus PETG gedruckt wird dann zu PLA wechseln) Daher kommen auch ein paar wenige Filamentwechsel. Wer dies möchte einfach das Profil normale Stützen drucken. Ich habe insgesamt 5 Modelle gedruckt bis das Getriebe die finale Version hattte. Viel Spaß damit! english version: This gearbox is part of a project from the “Design Engineering IV” course in our degree program. I developed the gear together with @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas and two other colleagues. We submitted this in addition to our term paper and are incredibly proud of it. It’s a wonderful demonstration model that has been further optimized beyond the original version we submitted. Here’s the key information about the gearbox: - The planetary gearbox is part of a press’s drive train. Surrounding the gearbox is a significantly larger flywheel, as well as a clutch. - I printed the gearbox entirely out of PLA; I don’t know how it would behave with other materials. - I used a Bambulab P1S and selected very fine settings. I’m not sure if that was necessary. In any case, the result is definitely impressive. - I wouldn’t scale the gearbox, as doing so would proportionally increase the distances between the bearings and the shaft, which are designed to be precisely matched. - To build a complete gearbox, you need to print plates 1–3 and either 4 or 5. Plate 4 includes a support with space for a label (see the PDF); plate 5 includes a support without space for a label. - According to my color coding: white is the drive shaft, black is the output shaft of the planetary carrier, gray is the housing, red is the gears, green is the bearings, and yellow is the plugs or screws - I glued the following parts in place: the pins into the housing, the plug into the housing, and the inner bearings directly to the housing - The covers can be glued to the housing, but then the gearbox can no longer be taken apart. The clip is there to keep the gearbox together anyway. It can be slid onto the entire housing from below - The small bearings are very difficult to press into the gears. To do this, gently tap them into the gears with a small tool until the bearings are clearly below the edge of the gear. - The cover of the planetary carrier has a special cutout so you can see a gear. The “screws”—which are actually just pins—were very difficult for me to insert. If you want to be able to open the gearbox easily again, it’s best to scale these down slightly and possibly glue them to the cover of the planetary carrier - The attached PDF contains the label (52mm x 22mm); I printed this on paper (DIN A4), which can be used as a sticker. However, you can also print them on regular paper and stick them on. - The entire gearbox with the frame requires about 130g of filament. - I used the Super Cool Track Pro plate for the housing and the Textured PEI Plate for the rest. That’s how it’s set up. If you use different plates, be sure to take this into account! - I used a few layers of “Support for PLA” for the supports under the housing. If you don't have “Support for PLA” filament, simply switch to PETG. It works just the same. (If the gearbox is printed in PETG, switch to PLA.) That's why there are a few filament changes. If you don't want those, just change the support settings in the slicer back to normal supports. I printed a total of 5 models before the gearbox reached its final version. Have fun with it!

I used a heavy piece of 1.5" thick painted particle board, which adds enough weight that you can insert the pin easily. It also makes putting the launcher at an angle much safer, if you are going for distance or competing with the wind. Later we took the setup to a large park, and the launcher was instantly set up and secured with the added weight of the base. The print profile includes a plate that uses a modifier part to increase the infill around the mounting hole. I printed one without this reinforcement and it worked perfectly, but for an extra 3 minutes and less than a gram of filament, you get a little extra insurance against over tightening your screw and crushing the walls of the print. This is by far the best launching system I have seen, and it was quick and efficient to print. Highly recommended. With these updated feet mounted to a heavy base, setup is quick and easy, regardless of location.

This is a fully 3D-printable, highly optimized Flat Box designed by default for the Sharpstar 61EDPH II refractor (90mm dew shield). The entire main body prints vertically without a single support structure! Built-in LED Channel: The main light chamber is specifically widened by 2mm per side. DC 5.5x2.1mm Male Power Pigtail Cable (30cm) — to plug the flat box directly into your ZWO ASIAIR 12V outputs. Bring a piece of mathematical history to your desk! Long before electronic calculators and computers, engineers and scientists used the slide rule to design everything from bridges to the Apollo rockets. This 3D-printable model uses a sliding mechanism based on logarithmic scales to perform multiplication and division. It’s a fantastic educational tool, a great conversation starter, and a fun puzzle for your brain. 🧮 How to Use It (Multiplication Example) Using a slide rule is simple once you get the hang of it: Find your first number on the stationary outer scale (D). Align the beginning "1" (the index) of the sliding inner scale (C) with that number. Look for your second number on the sliding scale (C). Read the final result directly opposite it on the outer scale (D). 💡 Want to dive deeper into the history and advanced functions (like division or square roots)? The location name is oriented so that the top of the frame aligns with the map's north orientation. To save filament, the frame's interior floor does not include a top layer; you can then secure the map in place using glue or another adhesive. The map frame is only 0.5mm larger in each direction, which makes for a nice fit. However, if your printer struggles with these smaller tolerances, feel free to scale up. CMS Rocket Assembly and Guidance Elevate Your Launch Experience with the 6-Fin Dual-Stage Rocket This carefully designed 6-fin dual-stage rocket can reach impressive altitudes exceeding 1,000 feet. Weighing just 120 grams at launch, including hardware, you can construct it from various materials, such as PLA, PETG, nylon, and ABS. This rocket combines durability and performance. Aerodynamic Design - Features an ergonomic nose cone and carefully designed fins for optimal stability in flight. Safe Recovery System - Includes dedicated parachute storage to ensure a reliable descent. Proven Performance - Successfully tested with openrocket and flown with C6-0 and B6-4 motors and built for multiple flights. Ideal for both novice and experienced rocketry enthusiasts, this rocket is a must-have for anyone looking to enhance their launching experience. In order to launch, you will need a launchpad/kit, 1 C6-0 motor (Estes) for the bottom stage, and a B6-4 for the top stage, as well as a parachute or streamer to find your rocket. Lastly, and VERY IMPORTANT!!! , the rocket needs exactly 3 pennies (~8 grams) in the nosecone to ensure the optimal ratio between the center of pressure and the center of gravity, so the rocket doesn't flip and shoot into the ground. Atmos Mk 1.2 The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a compact 3D-printable model rocket designed for use with Estes E16-6 and E16-8 motors . It features a dedicated electronics bay that can fit a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2 , GY-BME280 pressure sensor , and a 3.7V LiPo battery , allowing makers to add custom flight computers, altitude logging, and other experimental electronics. Designed with accessibility and customization in mind, the Atmos Mk 1.2 can be printed using a wide range of common 3D printing materials. Whether printed in PLA for easy prototyping, PETG for added durability, or other materials for specialized builds, the design can be adapted to suit different launch goals. The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a platform for makers, students, and rocketry enthusiasts who want to explore 3D printing, electronics, and experimental flight systems in a compact and reusable rocket design. Flight Notes Stability margin: Approximately 1.7 calibers . Estimated altitude: Typically reaches 800–1,000 ft (240–305 m) , depending on launch conditions. Flight history: Successfully tested over 3 flights (with a 4th planned) with E16-8 estes rocket motors, demonstrating reliable performance and durable construction, you could use f motors but i wouldn't go below 15N of force engines to ensure safe liftoff. Recommendations: do not attempt to remove the motor directly after flight wait for the plastic to cool read assembly note carefully to prevent hardware issues higher temp materials ensure more durability but i have printed out of both pla and petg for this project and pla will function and work I assembled a flight computer out of a raspberry pi pico a gy bme barometer and a small quadcopter battery for under ten dollars and this platform was mostly designed to test it i encourage others to do the same but also i plan to drop links to my functioning code later once i have it all ironed out Assembly Notes To assemble the Atmos Mk 1.2, you'll need 3–4 pennies, super glue, a nylon or Kevlar shock cord, a small amount of duct tape, recovery wadding, a small i hook, and your choice of recovery system (streamer or parachute) . The rocket is designed for Estes E16-6 or E16-8 motors . The nose cone includes a dedicated ballast pocket: Payload under 15 g: Glue 4 pennies into the nose cone. Payload over 15 g: Glue 3 pennies into the nose cone. For the best flight performance, try to keep payloads under 30 g . Secure your electronics using M3 screws, electrical tape, or both —tape alone works well for most builds, but using both provides maximum security. If any printed parts fit loosely, adjust the tolerances with a small amount of Scotch tape as needed. Finally, don't forget to add recovery wadding before every launch. Vou ser sincero. Eu nunca entendi por que esse dinossauro ficou tão famoso. Na minha opinião, a cabeça dele é enorme, desproporcional e o design inteiro parece ter sido feito às pressas. Existem centenas de dinossauros articulados melhores por aí que nunca receberam nem 1% da atenção que esse recebeu. Mas não foi isso que me trouxe aqui. O que me trouxe aqui foi descobrir que uma versão desse modelo está sendo vendida por absurdos R$100 apenas porque foi associada ao nome de alguém famoso. E quando uma pessoa decidiu disponibilizar uma alternativa gratuita para a comunidade, recebeu ameaças e pressão para apagar o arquivo. Dozy vive en los Árboles Altos del Oeste, donde avanza tan despacio que a veces tarda un día entero en cambiar de rama. Le gusta tomarse su tiempo, porque dice que los árboles cuentan mejor las cosas cuando nadie los apura. Una mañana empezó a trepar por un tronco cubierto de musgo. Al caer la tarde seguía allí, y justo entonces vio algo que otros no habían notado: a distintas horas del día, la luz iba marcando pequeñas líneas en la corteza, una tras otra, hasta formar la misma curva del camino antiguo. Así entendió una pequeña parte del misterio. Algunas pistas de Zoora no están escondidas por el lugar, sino por el momento: solo aparecen completas cuando se les da el tiempo que necesitan. Desde entonces, Dozy ya no siente que vaya tarde. Ahora sabe que avanzar despacio también puede ayudarte a ver lo que otros pasan por alto. Moraleja: No todo llega tarde por ir lento; a veces ir despacio es justo lo que te permite entenderlo.

Henny vive en Puerto Migaja, cerca de la panadería donde siempre caen pequeñas migas dulces al amanecer. Le encanta picotear el suelo con cuidado, porque dice que hasta una miga puede contar por dónde ha pasado alguien. Una mañana encontró varias migas azules junto a la puerta de la despensa. No estaban esparcidas al azar: formaban una línea muy fina que iba hacia una rendija bajo el suelo. Henny picoteó la madera tres veces y la rendija dejó escapar un soplo de aire salado. Entonces entendió algo importante: quien se llevó la llave de cobre no entró por la puerta de la panadería. Había llegado desde abajo, por una ruta escondida que conectaba Puerto Migaja con el camino antiguo. Desde entonces, Henny aprendió a no culpar al primer rastro que veía, porque en Zoora las respuestas a veces llegan por donde nadie estaba mirando. Update: keychain versions added on Plate 2 of each print profile! Rainbow trout are a member of the salmon family distinguished by dark green, pink, and white coloration with black spots. Originally native to to the Pacific basin, including eastern Russia, the Aleutian islands, Alaska, western Canada, and the west coast of the United stated, they have been introduced to many other waterways worldwide. In the US in the 1800's a government stocking program started stocking these prized game fish in lakes, rivers, and streams across the country. For this reason, rainbow trout are typically the first trout caught by young anglers (myself included). Rainbow trout come in many forms and subspecies. steelhead are a type that will live out at sea but return to the streams they were born in to spawn. Redbands are subspecies set apart by the vibrant red coloration of their lateral line. Palamino, golden, or banana trout are gold in color but still keep their pink lateral line. This subspecies originated from a single color mutation discovered in a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 that is still propagated to this day. These cold water fish usually weigh between 1-5lbs. This model is the newest edition to my articulated fish collection. Same interlocking scales, same assembly, same swimming motion. The fish were designed to fit on a single A1-mini plate, but can be scaled up as large as you want. These fish are colorful and for 3D printing that means there's going to be a lot of purging and filament swaps. To reduce the number of swaps, I've included a non-spotted version to eliminate an additional color change on almost every layer. Just use a thin paintbrush and black acrylic paint to paint the dots on the model after printing. Advantage: less waste, no bleeding of black into white Disadvantage: acrylic paint is water soluble so the dots could be washed off. I hope you enjoy your new fishy friend, happy printing (and fishing)!

Narly vive en el océano de Zoora, cerca de las corrien tes frías que llegan hasta los Muelles Fríos. Le gusta nadar despacio bajo el hielo, porque dice que el agua fría guarda mejor los secretos. Una mañana notó que su cuerno vibraba cada vez que pasaba cerca de una corriente muy estrecha. No era una corriente normal: iba y volvía por el mismo lugar, como si estuviera esperando a que alguien la reconociera. Narly la siguió con calma y entendió algo importante. La brújula de Cangüi no señalaba solo una isla lejana; señalaba el inicio de una ruta escondida que el océano aún recordaba. description: About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Entonces pasó algo extraño: la piedra vibró bajo él y, por un instante, apareció completa la línea que antes parecía quedar abierta en el gran círculo del camino antiguo . Así Chomp entendió una parte del misterio. La línea no estaba rota ni faltaba un trozo: simplemente solo se completaba cuando alguien presionaba los tres puntos al mismo tiempo. Desde entonces, Chomp ya no intenta esconder sus pasos. Ahora sabe que su fuerza no siempre complica las cosas; a veces también puede ayudar a resolverlas. Moraleja: A veces, eso que creías un problema es justo lo que hacía falta.

Beaky vive en los Árboles Altos del Oeste , donde le encanta observar los colores de las frutas y recordar en qué orden aparecen. Dice que, cuando algo se repite muchas veces, no siempre es casualidad. Una mañana vio tres frutas caídas sobre distintas ramas: una amarilla, una naranja y una roja. Más adelante encontró otras tres en el mismo orden. Y un poco más lejos, también. Beaky siguió aquel patrón hasta un árbol hueco muy antiguo. Al asomarse dentro, vio una línea azul muy tenue que bajaba por el tronco y desaparecía bajo la tierra. Entonces entendió una pequeña parte del misterio: en esa zona de Zoora, el camino antiguo pasaba justo bajo los árboles, y el bosque marcaba su recorrido con señales sencillas para quien supiera fijarse. Desde entonces, Beaky ya no se guarda lo que descubre. Cuando encuentra una pista, la anuncia enseguida, porque sabe que algunas señales sirven más cuando alguien las comparte. Moraleja: Descubrir algo importante está bien, pero compartirlo puede ayudar todavía más.

Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version.
