Hier werden sowohl das Bauteil als auch die Stützstruktur aus demselben Material gedruckt- in meinem Fall PETG Falls dir das Modell gefällt, freue ich mich über einen Like, einen Download, einen Boost und natürlich über Fotos deiner Drucke! This is a remixed model originally created by the very talented morph91 . Original model link: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2749412-bc-250-gaming-pc-case-mk-ultra-uno . I'm naming this model the MK Ultra Uno Plus : ) This model can be printed in three plates with less than 600g of filament, and is a completely tool-less design like the original (no screws are required). Unlike the original, I adapted the design to work with three of the most popular flex psu's for the BC250. The FSP500-30AS, Apevia ITX flex, and Metalfish flex psus are all compatible with this remix. Important Considerations: There are three different versions of the back half of the case. Each one fits the different compatible psus. Please make sure you only print the plate for your psu! There are two different versions of the fan shroud. One is the exact same as the original, the other is a modified version that allows active airflow to flow to stick on heatsinks that I personally made for my build. You can reference the assembly instructions for photos. Please make sure you only print the plate relevant for your build! Both the apevia and metalfish variants of the back case contain one less internal clip/latch due to space constraints. so these variants may be slightly less rigid when the two case halves are put together The internal psu lock has only been confirmed working for the FSP500-30AS psu. You may need to modify/create your own internal psu lock for the apevia/metalfish psus If anyone ends up printing the apevia or metalfish variants, please let me know if anything needs to be adjusted! I used morph91 's measurements for the metalfish variant and also lolheyaj 's measurements for the apevia variant, since I do not personally own either of those psus. Also, I welcome anyone to create internal psu locks for those two variants : ) Here's a list of all the modifications I did to the original: Changed front face design Changed front to use 12mm button Changed rear side design (small holes similar to actual pc cases) Removed rear side external psu latch and changed to internal psu lock instead (confirmed only for fsp500-30as so far) Changed back design to fit FSP500-30AS Created another variant of back half of case to fit apevia flex psu Created another variant of back half of case to fit metalfish flex psu Changed back design to fit 40mm exhaust fan(s) Added interior clips/latches to connect the two halves of the case more securely Added stick on heatsinks next to fan shroud Changed fan shroud to have a small slit allowing for active airflow to the added heatsinks (this improved temps by 3-7C ingame with 40CU unlock and 2000MHz GPU OC) Expected Thermals: WIP. So far it's mostly been in the 60C range in games like crimson desert, portal 2, hogwarts legacy, and hades (gpu 40CU 2000MHz undervolted to 900mV, cpu stock). My Part List: BC250 PSU (fsp500-30as, apevia itx flex, or metalfish flex) makerworld.com/en/models/2527214-bc-250-scooper fin scooper to straighten fins https://a.co/d/0hZ28ifs for 12mm latching button (you may need a wire stripper, wire crimper, and dupont connectors if you copy me 1:1) https://a.co/d/0jdT5jNV arctic p12 pro pst (optional) https://a.co/d/063cMg66 noctua NF-A4x20 (optional) https://a.co/d/00RnzoEo stick on heatsinks, I bought 2 of these kits and used 3 out of the 4 heatsinks (optional) This looks to be a cheaper alternative: https://a.co/d/038s6cPO - it would be the same size as what I used, but as one large piece instead. Based on reviews, it looks like a thermal pad of some sort is already preapplied. If you end up buying this one, let me know how it fits! (optional) https://a.co/d/066uYDJ8 rubber anti vibration screws used to mount noctua 40mm fan Print Instructions: Print in PETG, and dry filament for 8 hours before printing (reduces stringing). Make sure to print only one of the fan shroud plates, and one of the back case plates. For more information read the important considerations at the top. The front case fits all the back case variants. If you are downloading the model to modify or use with a different slicer (and not bambu studio), then make sure to paint a straight line seam on the bottom part of back half of the case. This helps reduce VFAs: Assembly Instructions: Take off the IO shield and the small bracket next to cmos battery Use the fin scooper to straighten the fins underneath where the fan shroud is gonna go. After straightening the fins, use an air duster to make sure any debris is blown off. Also if you haven't already, repaste the chip - it lowered my temps by 5C! Attach fan (recommend arctic p12 pro pst) with pins to fan shroud. Then attach fan shroud to pcb. Make sure the two small latches are pushed as far up as possible (in pic below you can see the one latch is in the corner of the pcb). Optionally here, if you have the stick on heatsinks (120x40x20mm), you can stick them right next to the fan slit. Doing this mod helped my ingame temps by 3-7C. VERY IMPORTANT NOTE: If you do not have/don't plan to use stick on heatsinks print the plate with the original fan shroud instead! Put PSU into back half of case: Add psu lock on left side (currently only known compatible for fsp500-30as): Mount any 40mm fans now (both screws or rubber mounts work): Slide bc250 on alu backplate onto the back half of case. Plug in exhaust fan to the Y splitter of main fan. Plug in the 8 pin power cable: (This step is for FSP500-30AS psu, idk what pins to short for apevia/metalfish psus but you can probably find out on reddit) Plug in latching button to PS_ON and GND. I crimped the wires into two male dupont connectors and put them in a 2pin housing. I slightly have to bend the metal pins to fit into the psu which creates enough friction where the pins don't fall out. There's probably a better solution for this… Attach front half of case, and slide until both halves attach together. Enjoy!

CUSTOMIZABLE DIY FILAMENT/BOOK SHELF SEVERAL RISER OPTIONS CUSTOMIZE TO FIT YOUR SPACE NOTE: REQUIRES SOME WORK WITH WOOD As part of my new print room, I designed this DIY shelf system to maximize the space I had available for my filament storage dry boxes and keep them organized. At the same time l wanted something truly unique and nice to look at. I decided to share it here in case others want to try it themselves. Please read all of the information and the attached instructions before starting. Overall, it may not be a huge cost savings compared to an Ikea or other purchasable bookshelf (though the larger it is the more it will save), but being able to make it the exact length and height you want is not possible with those options. Plus, the looks of this are so much better IMO. The riser options include: Diamondplate Pattern Lattice Pattern Square & Compass Vertical Bolts (these are only recommended for middle risers) FYI If you are interested in the filament labels or drybox kits shown in the pictures, you can find them here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/1193463-filament-labels-with-logos https://makerworld.com/en/models/2561229-4l-dry-box-kit-for-outer-spool-desiccant-trays ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ PURCHASED PARTS SHELVES The shelves themselves are made of ¾” wood and the risers are designed to fit a shelf depth of 234mm (9-3/8”). Your shelf length will be whatever length you want for your needs (more on that in the instructions below). This means you can source the shelving a number of different ways. Buy standard ¾” shelf boards and trim them to size. The ends are covered and the back not visible so you could get them pre-finished if you can make clean cuts. Buy a ¾” MDF sheet and cut or have the hardware store cut to the correct depth and whatever length you decide, then paint as needed. This is the option I chose. Buy a ¾” plywood sheet and cut or have the hardware store cut to the correct depth and whatever length you decide. Then you would need to add edging to the front edge to cover the layer lines before painting. HARDWARE Threaded wood inserts – ¼” or M6 x ¾” or 20mm (9) Inserts are required PER SHELF I used these: https://a.co/d/0hchaaFy Flattened or Button Head Screws – ¼”x1-1/2” or M6x35 (18) screws per intermediate shelf, (9) screws per top and bottom shelf I used these: https://a.co/d/00rvAgmG IF you are going to use the Square and Compass Risers, you will also need (4) M5 heat press inserts (any length up to 12mm max) and (4) M5x20mm Socket Head Screws PER RISER to connect the pieces together. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PRINTED PARTS You will need the following printed parts from the print profile of your choice: RISERS – Selection and quantity are up to you. Generally, you will need 2 risers per shelf and if you feel it needs a middle riser. Bolt Risers are only recommended as a middle riser and require 3 per riser. Square and Compass Risers include 3 pieces per riser that need assembled – main riser, top, and bottom. RISER CONNECTORS – These slide onto the shelf and connect to the risers. You will need 2 side connectors (and 1 middle connector if you chose a middle riser) per shelf. The top shelf has special Top Riser Connectors. Bolt Risers do not need any Riser Connectors but are only recommended as a middle riser. BOLT SPACERS – These get bolted to the shelves to interconnect the risers and riser connectors. You will need the same quantity as the screws – 18 per intermediate shelf, 9 per top and bottom shelf. FEET - You can attach any feet of your liking to the bottom using the ¼" threaded holes. The ones in the picture which I recommend I had previously released here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2498728-hd-adjustable-leveling-foot Now let’s talk about print orientation. There are 2 print profiles – one with the risers and connectors oriented flat on the bed, and one with risers and connectors oriented vertically. Depending on your filament of choice, printing orientation will change how the color looks. Square & Compass Risers and Bolt Risers must be printed vertically unless you are willing to get creative with supports. Vertical printing creates a higher resolution but is much more challenging to print. The hardest part with vertical printing is the Riser Connectors because the opening for the shelf requires supports. You can use a special support material but this adds layer time which can cause a “benchy hull” line from the big difference in layer time. Not using special support material (like I didn’t) creates a rough interface. Not too big of a deal since it is sitting flat against the shelf, but I had to make little trim pieces to cover the exposed outer edge. Those are included if you need them. If you like the look or the filament color doesn't change, another option would be to print the risers vertically and the connectors flat. This would be kind of the “best of both worlds”. I chose a shiny filament, so orientation made a big difference in the color. Here is a comparison of the two print orientations: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- FILAMENT SELECTION The majority of the loading is in compression (buckling) so material requirements aren’t too bad. I recommend a MINIMUM of a PLA+ that has decent impact strength. A good Tough PLA+ like the one Bambu has, Sunlu’s PLA+ 2.0, or Polymaker Polylite PLA PRO would be decent options. I would avoid basic matte or silk PLA’s as their brittleness and layer adhesion may not make it appropriate. PETG will generally hold up a little better but is more difficult to print. I chose Tinmorry Space Grey Metallic PETG because it gave me a nice “steel” look and I printed vertically. Seams and retraction were a big challenge however and took me a couple tries. I have attached the assembly instruction and basic assembly dimensions. Length is based on the one I built and fit the dry boxes shown in the pictures perfectly, but you can adjust to the length you want for your needs. Thank you and if you decide to do this project, I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

This helps me out and helps supporting this project with since i could not upload the Bambuplot file directly on Makerworld. ⚠ Read this first this is a tinkerer's project This tool is made for people who enjoy experimenting, troubleshooting, and figuring things out. It is not a plug-and-play product. It will probably not work perfectly on the first try , and that is completely normal. Getting a pen plotter working on a 3D printer requires patience: dialing in the Z height, finding the right pen, getting the paper flat, tuning the feed rates, and sometimes just accepting that the first few attempts are learning runs. I do not cover any damages to your printer, pen holder, bed, or any other part of your setup. Using this tool is entirely at your own risk. Sending custom G-code to a 3D printer always carries a risk of unexpected movement, crashes, or damage if settings are wrong. Always supervise the printer, always do a dry run first with the Z height raised so the pen cannot touch anything, and never leave it running unattended especially not on a first test. If you are not comfortable with that, this project is probably not for you yet but if you enjoy the process of making something work from scratch, welcome aboard. What is BambuPlot? BambuPlot is a single HTML file you download and open in your browser. It lets you design drawings and convert them into G-code that your Bambu Lab printer can execute with a pen instead of a nozzle. No internet connection is required after download — it runs 100% on your computer. Supported printers all current Bambu Lab models: Printer Bed size Notes A1 mini 180 × 180 mm A1 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested P1P 256 × 256 mm P1S 256 × 256 mm P2S 256 × 256 mm X1 carbon 256 × 256 mm X2D 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested A2L 330 × 320 mm H2D 325 × 320 mm H2S 340 × 320 mm A custom bed size option is also available for any other setup. What you can draw: Text three modes: single-stroke plotter font (looks like real handwriting), your own custom handwriting (draw each letter yourself, up to 5 versions per letter for variety so repeating letters never look identical), or filled outline using any of 13 fonts Shapes square, circle, triangle, star, line, with optional hatch fill Freehand draw directly on the bed preview with your mouse or stylus Images drop any photo or logo, adjust the threshold and line density, and convert it to plotted lines 3MF import drop a Bambu Lab .3mf file and BambuPlot extracts the 3D geometry and renders the top-down footprint as plottable paths, in either vector outline or hatch-fill mode What you need A Bambu Lab printer or anything else that takes gcode A pen holder that mounts on your toolhead (search MakerWorld or Printables for your specific model many free designs exist) A ballpoint pen that fits your holder Paper to draw on, attached to the bed (see bed preparation below) A way to get pure gcode on your printer (USB stick/microsd) Bed preparation protecting your print surface This is important. The pen tip will press directly down onto whatever is on your bed. Printing on bare paper placed directly on a softer printing bed can cause damage, especially with a stiff pen or too much Z pressure. My recommendation: place an old flat PEI sheet (Like mine from my old ender 3 v2), a thin sheet of plastic such as a folder cover or binder sheet, or any similarly flat, smooth piece of thin plastic underneath the paper. This gives the paper a firm, even surface to rest on and takes any wear from the pen instead of your actual print bed. An old or scratched PEI sheet you no longer use for printing is perfect for this. Attaching the paper: I use small magnets placed along the edges to hold the paper flat and in position they are quick to place, leave no residue, and hold very reliably. Other options that work fine include masking tape or binder clips on the edges. Whatever you use, make sure the paper is completely flat with no bubbles or lifted corners, as any unevenness will cause the pen pressure to vary across the drawing. How to download and open BambuPlot Go to : https://joep648.github.io/BambuPlot/bambuplot-v1.0.1.html to use it online. or Download the bambuplot.html file from: https://github.com/Joep648/BambuPlot/tree/main Open it with any modern browser (Firefox recommended for best performance Chrome and Edge work fine too, but Firefox handles large designs more smoothly) That is it no installation, no internet needed after that Step-by-step: from design to plot Step 1 Select your printer In the top bar, choose your printer model from the dropdown. The bed preview updates to the correct size. This ensures your G-code coordinates match your actual print surface. Step 2 Add content to the bed Use the tabs on the left panel: Text tab type your text, choose a style (single-stroke is best for plotting), adjust letter spacing and line spacing, then click Add text to bed Shapes tab pick a shape and click Add shape to bed . Enable Filled to get hatch-fill lines inside the shape Image tab click the drop zone or drag an image in. Adjust the threshold slider until the preview looks like clean black lines on white, then click Convert & add to bed . High-contrast line art like the included boat image gives the best results 3MF tab drag a .3mf file onto the drop zone. Choose Vector outline for a clean single-stroke contour of the model, or Top-down silhouette for a hatch-filled footprint Freehand in the Shapes tab, click Draw directly on bed and sketch with your mouse Step 3 Position and size your content Once an item appears on the bed preview: Drag the body of the item to move it Drag a corner handle to scale it the line density automatically recalculates to stay consistent at the new size Drag the white circle above the item to rotate it Use the Layers tab to show/hide, duplicate, or delete items Step 4 Configure pen settings Go to the Pen tab and set: Setting What it does Suggested starting value Z draw How far down the pen tip presses 0.5 mm Z lift How high the pen lifts between strokes 8 mm Draw feed Speed while drawing 1500 mm/min Travel feed Speed while moving between strokes 6000 mm/min Z move feed Speed of Z moves 600 mm/min Pen settle time Dwell after each Z move to prevent stray marks 120 ms These values are starting points every pen holder and pen combination is different. Adjust Z draw until the pen just barely touches the paper with light pressure. Step 5 Generate and download the G-code Click Generate G-code in the right panel. The code appears in the preview (large designs only show the first few thousand lines the full file is always in the download). Click the ⭳ button to download the .gcode file. Step 6 Send to the printer and plot My personal workflow: Home the printer manually via the touchscreen or Bambu Studio After homing, clip the pen holder onto the toolhead with the pen inserted Place your protective plastic sheet on the bed, lay the paper on top, and secure it with magnets, tape, or clips Start the file with in bambuplot Home all axes (G28) at start option turned off Always do a dry run first: temporarily raise the Z draw value by 5–10 mm so the pen stays off the paper, and watch the full motion to confirm the design lands in the right place before doing a real plot Alternative workflow using the dwell option: The Dwell after homing checkbox in the Pen tab inserts a G4 S30 command (a timed pause) after the G28 home command, giving you time to clip the pen on before plotting starts. This feature is experimental and untested I have not personally used it this way. Bambu printers do not support the standard M0 unconditional pause command, so a timed dwell is used as a workaround. If you try it, set the duration long enough to comfortably attach the pen holder (60 seconds or more). Tips for best results Use the right paper smooth, slightly heavier paper works best. Thin paper can wrinkle from pen pressure Ballpoint pens are the most reliable. Felt-tips can bleed on paper and dry out if the pen sits in one spot for too long Start with a short test plot a small shape first to calibrate your Z height before committing to a full design Line density matters lower density (higher number on the slider) = fewer lines = faster plot and less ink bleed. Higher density looks more solid but takes much longer to plot The settle time setting (default 120 ms) adds a brief pause after every pen up/down move. This is the main fix for random stray lines on the paper if you see faint marks between strokes, increase it to 150–250 ms Mirror X or Y if your plot comes out flipped Saving your settings In the Pen tab, click Save profile + handwriting to file to save all your pen settings, printer choice, and your custom drawn handwriting alphabet to a single .json file. Load it again any time even on a different device with the load button. Questions, problems, and ideas for future versions If something does not work, you have a question about the setup, or you just want to share your results feel free to leave a comment on this MakerWorld page or send me a message directly through MakerWorld. I am happy to help where I can, though keep in mind this is a hobby project and responses may not always be instant. If you have ideas for features you would like to see in a future version, I would love to hear them. BambuPlot is actively being worked on and new features get added regularly. Things on the radar include better SVG import, more letter styles, and improved multi-layer support. If there is something specific you need for your use case, suggest it in the comments the best ideas from the community are what shape where this goes next. BambuPlot is a fan-made tool and is not affiliated with Bambu Lab. Pen holder designs are not included search MakerWorld or Printables for a mount that fits your specific printer model. Always run a dry pass before plotting on good paper. Use at your own risk.

description: Hallo Druckfreunde! Heute teile ich meine Silika Gel Box für Vakuumbeutel . Feuchtigkeit ist ja bekanntlich der größte Feind von perfektem 3D-Druck. Warum dieses Design den Unterschied macht: Smarte Slicer-Optimierung: Die Wände dieses Behälters werden flach liegend gedruckt. Das sorgt für einen schnellen, stabilen und druckerschonenden Druckprozess. Funktionales Gyroid-Infill: Durch das Weglassen von Deck- und Bodenschichten wird das Gyroid-Infill als hochfunktionale Außenhaut genutzt. Das Ergebnis: Eine perfekte 360°-Durchlüftung für die Silikakugeln, ohne dass diese herausfallen. Visuelle Feuchtigkeitskontrolle auf einen Blick: Wenn du transparentes Filament für das Infill verwendest, kannst du den Zustand deiner Silikakugeln (Farbwechsel bei Sättigung) perfekt durch das Gyroid-Muster hindurch ablesen – direkt durch den Vakuumbeutel, ohne ihn extra öffnen zu müssen! Platzsparend & Effizient: Nutzt den ungenutzten Raum in der Mitte der Filament-Spule optimal aus und ersetzt die meist schon gesättigten Silkapäckchen. Gedruckt habe ich die Box in zwei Farben (macht ein AMS notwendig) und mit PETG . Ich empfehle PETG, da es flexibel und robust für den Einsatz mit Silika Gel ist. Die sichtbare Gyroid Schicht ist mit einem transparenten PETG gedruckt. Desweiteren gibt es auf Druckplatte 2 einen kleinen Helfer, der euch bei der Montage unterstützt. Dieser kann auch mit PLA gedruckt werden und ist für die Funktion der Box nicht notwendig. Montagehinweis: druckt alle nötigen Teile für den Behäler aus druckt den ‘Helper’ aus schiebt den ‘Helper’ über das Grundgerüst, wie im Bild unten zu sehen biegt die Wände leicht vor und schiebt sie dann, durch die Führung, bis in den Boden dann noch den Deckel einschrauben, gerade aufsetzen… fertig!!!

description: I created this low-profile, high-flow X2D downward-facing exhaust adapter for a compact air filtration unit. (I will be posting the full unit on MakerWorld soon as well!) I printed and tested some of the other low-profile exhausts on MakerWorld, but they either restricted the airflow too much or didn't fit my specific use case. To ensure optimal performance, I simulated the airflow of my model in SOLIDWORKS Flow Simulation (visible in the attached images). While it’s obviously not perfect given the tight space restrictions, it's the absolute best path for the air to travel. This partitioning allows easy modification of any component without needing to reprint the other components. For example, the Hose Adapter can be easily replaced to support different hose sizes. Let me know in the comments the Inner Diameter (ID) of the particular hose that you need. Assembly Base Assembly The first step is to assemble the Fan Vent Base. The two types of clips (as shown in Figure 1 ) are inserted into the Fan Vent Base (Low Profile Fan Vent P2S V4.stl) in the positions indicated in Figure 2 . First install the Latch Body part ( Figure 3 ) on the fan Module connector, then insert two BT2x5 self-tapping screws as indicated by the green arrows and tighten them on the both sides to attach it to the Latch Body. Note: The screws act as shafts. Do not over-tighten them otherwise the Latch will not work smoothly. Figure 3 : Latch Body Installation Next install the Latch Latch part ( Figure 4 ) on the fan Module connector, then insert two BT2x5 self-tapping screws as indicated by the green arrows and tighten them on the both sides to attach it to the Latch Body. Figure 4 : Latch Latch Installation Now use the same process to attach the Latch components on the opposite of the Fan Module for the Base, and on the top and bottom of the Fan Module for the Hose Adapter, as shown in Figure 5 . Figure 5 : Hose Adapter Latches Fan Installation Before continuing remove any leftover support material from around the inside of the Connector Holes ( Figure 6 ) and the ‘top’ inside surface of the PCB case (as indicated by the blue arrow in Figure 6 ). model_name: Low Profile P2S Chamber Exhaust Fan Kit ver1.0
description: This is a lower profile Chamber Exhaust Fan than the official Bambu “ P2S Chamber Exhaust Fan Kit ”. It uses the same $20 Bambu P2S chamber exhaust fan kit parts . Though design may appear similar to the Original Bambu Chamber Exhaust Fan in some ways, it is an entirely different, scratch built design. This design is not in any way associated with Bambu, so use this design at your own risk. No warranties are given. This project was a collaboration with MadMopar (over on MakerWorld). MadMopar had the original idea for a lower profile exhaust duct for the P2S, ran multiple prototypes, provided suggestions and feedback to refine the design, and also provided all the images of the printed design. So a big thanks goes out to MadMopar ! PLEASE NOTE: This profile does not include the poop chute shown in the pics (and the baseplate included here is not compatible with that poop chute design). This model only includes a basic (flat) plate for the poop chute. If you want to use Mc2.project3D's “ Inspectable Waste Chute – Series P / X / H2 ” which is shown in the pics , you will be able to find a remixed backplate and slide which are compatible with that designat the link below (due to the MakerWorld Exclusive License): https://makerworld.com/en/models/2920654-baseplate-only-for-the-inspectable-waste-chute#profileId-3267976 Between MadMopar and myself, many hours have been spent polishing the design, testing and improving it. I feel it is completed, and the one of these ducts in operation currently (with the 2" duct) has been performing well. But if you make or use this design and see anything that could be improved, please provide feedback (positive or negative). I cannot guarantee that the changes will be made, but I will check the comments. I don't own the P2S myself, so if you have a problem, providing pics and accurate measurements would be very helpful. Functionally, this design differs from the official Bambu Chamber Exhaust Fan design in the following key ways: This design has a lower overall profile, which can help in setups with limited room behind the printer. This design uses magnets to hold the duct on, instead of the latches on the stock Bambu design. It was thought that the magnetic attachment would make the duct easier to install or remove when there is limited space behind the printer. This design shifts the whole Exhaust Fan to the left a few mm, which allows for more poop chute options. This does however move the poop chute mount a bit away from the printer, which could be a problem with some poop chute designs (YMMV). This design has an optional TPU gasket, or can be used with 1/16" (1.58mm) thick foam tape, between the backplate and printer, to reduce air leakage. This design does not have room for a HEPA filter , which the official Bambu Chamber Exhaust design does allow for. This design is strictly for venting the chamber either outside or to a separate air cleaner. This design is a bit more complex and expensive to build, since it uses 16x 10x3mm cylinder magnets to hold the duct on, and requires more filament. Currently there are only ducts for a 2" or 2.5" (inside diameter) hose, with options for ducts that angle out at 45°, 90° and straight out from the printer. The 2.5" ducts are untested , and you can find them at the following link: https://www.printables.com/model/1754424-25-ducts-for-bambu-p2s-and-p1-exhaust-see-descript I may add additional ducts in the future, but I plan to upload the STEP models for this design to help with remixing the design. I may upload this in the future to MakerWorld, so I kindly ask that you please do not upload this design to MakerWorld. Thanks for understanding. To build this, the following hardware is needed (in addition to the Bambu P2S Exhaust Fan Kit): 2x M3x20 FHCS (Flat Head Cap Screws) 2x M3x14 (upto 20mm long) FHCS 4x M5x10 Self-Tapping Case Fan Screws 16x 10x3mm Cylinder Magnets 1/16" foam tape (optional) and not needed if using the TPU Gasket Superglue Printing: There are two main profiles available for the main parts. One of the main profiles is set up for ABS and uses brims and mouse ears to help with bed adhesion. The other main profile is set up with PETG, and does not use brims. Both profiles use a textured build plate, however both also specify an Engineering Plate for the optional TPU gasket. The Engineering Plate for TPU is just a suggestion, but I recommend using a smoother plate with glue as a release agent, since TPU tends to aggressively stick to the textured plates. There are additional profiles for the 2" ducts. Any future duct sizes will also have a separate profile. The image below shows the layout of the profile. The only options, aside from the TPU gasket, are the three L-Clip choices. The L-Clips mount into the baseplate, and help to hold the vent fan to the back of the printer, along with 2 screws around the poop chute. The L-Clips are available in different lengths, depending on how the vent fan is configured. There are different L-Clip sizes for using 1/16" foam tape, the optional TPU gasket, or no tape and no TPU gasket (which will probably allow more leakage of air). These options are described below the image: Referring to the above image, the L-Clip options are: A. L-Clips used with 1/16" foam tape (plate 04) B. L-Clips used without the foam tape or TPU gasket (plate 05) C. L-Clips used with the TPU gasket on plate 06 (plate 04) The 3mf profiles included were set up using Bambu Studio v2.7.1.57 and include the following: 92mm_Fan_Cover_v95_PETG_no_Ducts.3mf (base profile without brims, for PETG) 92mm_Fan_Cover_v95_ABS_w_BRIMS_no_Ducts.3mf (base profile with brims, for ABS) v6Z_2in_Ducts_only.3mf (45°, 90°, dual, and straight through 2" ducts) V1F_2-5in_Ducts.3mf (UNTESTED 45°, 90°, and straight through 2" ducts) The individual STEP models will be added later, when the license is changed to allow for remixing. Assembly: First decide if you plan to use the optional TPU cover, or 1/16" foam tape before gathering the parts. This will determine which type of L-hook is used, and which plates need to be printed. See the above information under “Printing” to decide which size L-Clips you need to use. Start by installing the L-Clips into the baseplate. These will need a bit of glue to hold them in place. Next, remove the two screws around the poop chute. These will be re-installed in the following steps, through the baseplate. If the TPU cover (shown in orange) is going to be used, install it on the baseplate: Install the baseplate onto the back of the printer. First start the right side L-Clip hooks in the corresponding holes on the printer metal backplate, then start the left side hooks. When both are in place and the baseplate will sit flush to the printer, slide the baseplate leftward until it stops. At this point the holes on the plate should align with the holes for the screws around the poop chute which were removed in step 3. These two screws can now be re-installed through the baseplate to help secure it to the printer. Install 8 of the 10x3 cylinder magnets into the cover as shown. Pay special attention to the polarity of these magnets, and how they are installed, so they will attract the magnets which will be installed in the duct. It can help to mark one pole of the magnets with a sharpie before starting, so there is a visual indicator of their polarity. I recommend installing the magnets so the poles are all pointed in the same direction, which will make things easier later. A drop of superglue will help secure them. Install the fan into the cover of the printer, using the M5x10 self-tapping fan screws. Make sure the fan power cable wraps either around the top or bottom side of the fan, and will not become pinched. Connect the fan cable to the board from the P2S Exhaust Fan Kit. Use the 3 screws included with the P2S Exhaust Fan Kit to install the board into the cover. You can use the small wire management slot (circled in green) to manage the extra wire. Double check that the wiring is connected and none of the fan wires are pinched (or will get pinched during the next assembly steps). Install the cover (with the fan and board previously installed) onto the baseplate using the M3 flat head screws: Install 8 of the 10x3mm cylinder magnets into the fan duct. Pay special attention to the polarity of the magnets here, since they should all be set up to attract the magnets already installed in the fan cover. It may help to set the magnets onto the fan cover magnets, prior to installing, so you can verify they will attract and not repel. If your magnets are not all set up as north or south on the fan cover and duct, be sure to orient the duct in the final position before installing magnets in it, otherwise it may attract on some and repell on others. It can also help to mark one pole of the magnets with a sharpie before starting, so there is a visual indicator of their polarity. A drop of superglue may help them stay. Install the duct onto the fan cover. Please provide feedback on this design (positive or negative), so it can be improved, thanks! model_name: Light and Fast Dual AMS Mount for H/X/P Series
description: I wanted a mount that didn't take too long to print or require too much material so I designed a mount that utilizes the weight of the AMS itself to help the mount clamp against the machine and keep the structure light. Unfortunately, the machines are not exactly the overall dimensions that Bambu cites. To accommodate this, the structure is broken into pieces that can be connected at various lengths to accommodate various printer sizes. This also makes them compatible with various models of Bambu machines. I also managed to fit all the parts in a single X/P series bed. H2C/H2S/H2D P2S X1C /X1E P1S/P1P AMS 2 AMS (3 Cavity) AMS (5 Cavity) Verified X X X X X Compatible X X Incompatible Note for High Temp Users: High temp printing with chamber heating will heat the printer glass beyond the glass transition temperature of PLA. This will cause warping of the structure. Please print the mount from a high temp plastic if you plan on printing chamber heated materials. If you only print PLA, this should not be an issue. Here is how the structure works: AMS weight hanging over the edge of the machine pushes down, forcing supports to pivot around the edge of the machine. Supports are retained by central tension member, which drives force into the side of the machine. Forces driving into side of machine increase friction between support and machine, improving grip. Small nubs on the central support posts retain both AMS units against each other, and prevent them from moving when the printer shakes. Size the frames so they are snug to the machine. If the notches only allow a slightly loose or slightly tight fit, choose the tight one. Once the weight of the AMS is loaded on top, any bowing in the structure will flatten out. The assembly utilizes toothed connections which are finely tuned to slide together and retain themselves with the layer lines of the print. If parts are too tight, they can likely be tapped together with a hammer without issue, just dont expect to get them back apart. If too loose, you can scale just the tensioning rods (the thin rectangular parts) to 101% to get a tighter fit. This gif shows the assembly process:

description: Weirdly enough, I couldn't find a five color Benchy to test my H2C out! There are plenty of seven color Benchys, but the H2C only comes with five 0.4mm nozzles and a single AMS 2 Pro, meaning only 5 colors out of the box. Therefore, I've added five colors to the original Benchy all at a 45 degree angle to increase color changes, that way you can watch the H2C, a piece of engineering art, do it's magic. If you're curious of what the different coloring methods are in the print profile, I'll explain a bit more. The first plate in the print profile, colored by painting, was colored using Bambu Studio's paint tool. The paint tool is great, but can leave a rough seam between colors. That's why I also included a second option, colored by modifiers, which leaves a perfectly straight seam between colors. You won't be able to see the colors from the previewer for this method, but they are there. You can see the colors you want to use with the painted model, then print it out using the modifiers version.

I wanted to be able to quickly take out and put back in those containers to dry the desiccant. Once every few months I just take the silica containers out of all my boxes and put them in my AMS to dry on dry trays . And since I have a label maker I also added a slot for filament info cards so that I can see from outside exactly which filament is inside the boxes. model_name: Snapmaker U1 + Sunlu Filadryer S4 Feeder Adapter
description: Humidity, my worst enemy… Snapmaker sent me the U1, and unfortunately, I'm not able to get good prints with printers that have open-air spools (because of the humidity at my location). So I looked for the best way to deal with it, and none of the projects I found were good enough. The closest one used a Sunlu Filadryer S4, so that was my baseline to start this project: Snapmaker u1 + Sunlu Fliladryer S4 Setup Compact setup Air-tight (at least as much as the original S4) It has the feeders as close as possible to the spools → Easier loading and unloading This is a DIY project, so you will need some tools and materials: M3 x 6 Screws, 4 of them with nuts and washers 2 x PTFE connectors. The ones that allow the 4 mm PTFE tube to pass through Drills (3.5 mm for the screws, and one for the size of your PTFE connectors) Extra PTFE tubes (4 mm OD, 2.5 mm ID) to replace the ones that go from the original feeder location to the back of the printer. Feeder extension cable. This might be the trickiest. They can be found as GH1.25 or JST GH1.25. Be sure they are 15-pin and male-female configuration. The length depends on your setup; measure both sides from the feeder's original location to the back of the Sunlu S4. I recommend 50 cm. I'll leave some links in the comments. I don't have measurements of the process, because I did it on the go and wasn't planning to upload it anywhere. But I have some pictures taken from the video I recorded: Depending on your setup, you would want to place the S4 on the right or the left of the U1. Therefore, you need to install the feeders on the side of the S4 that faces the back (as shown in the pictures above). You need to measure the distance between the feeder inputs, and drill the holes in the S4 to install the PTFE connectors. Then, assemble the feeders in the printed holder, and place it with the holes aligned to the filament input. Mark the Holder holes, and drill the 3.5 mm holes for the screw assembly. Assemble it, place the numbers from the inside, and then the funnels (optional, but recommended) Then, place the U1 and S4 in the final position, measure, cut, and install the PTFE tubes from the printer to the feeder. Don't make them too short or they might bend; leave some extra for them to wiggle around with smooth curves. That's about it. As I said, I made it on the go, so I'm not sure if I'm forgetting something 😂

description: This highly-engineered, premium spool mounting system was designed exclusively and specifically for the Snapmaker U1 equipped with a Biqu PopCap . It uses print-in-place conical roller bearings to perfectly center and suspend your spools, providing a firm, stable hold and an easy spin that eliminates extruder drag. ✨ Key Features Smooth Conical Bearings: The spools ride on 60mm conical hubs that automatically self-center any filament spool (from standard Bambu/Polymaker sizes up to wide-bore spools). Built-in print-in-place dumbbell roller bearings make them spin incredibly easily. Premium Sweeping Design: No blocky, basic geometry here. The brackets feature a gorgeous, mathematically perfect sweeping crescent arch with rounded fillets that look like high-end injection molding. No Hardware Required: The entire assembly is 100% 3D printed. No metal skate bearings or screws needed! 🖨️ Printing Instructions I have provided a fully prepared .3mf print profile with all the parts perfectly oriented on the bed. No supports are needed! Infill: 15-20% Gyroid is plenty strong for the brackets. Material: PETG, ABS, or PLA+ (If your enclosure gets hot, avoid standard PLA for the brackets). 🔧 Assembly The Brackets: Simply slide the hook slots horizontally onto the top and bottom lip of your PopCap enclosure door. The Bearings: Slide the printed conical bearings onto the 14.6mm bracket axles. (Pro Tip: Use a small dab of superglue between the axle and the inner hole of the bearing to hold it permanently in place. This makes it way easier to push the cones against the spool without them slipping off!) 🤝 Remix Credit The incredibly smooth internal roller geometry of the conical bearings is powered by the brilliant parametric Print-in-Place Bearing Generator by Koolm. model_name: Will it stick? Adhesion / Warping Torture Test
description: Everyone runs their own warp/adhesion tests. Nobody else ever learns from them. Every time someone figures out whether a filament sticks to a plate, that answer stays in their head, and the next person burns time and filament rediscovering it. You end up getting people in discord or reddit or forums having their own tiny bit of anecdotal evidence, and everyone cargo cults it. Will It Stick fixes that: print one standard model, report what happened, and your result joins a free, searchable matrix of build plate × filament × surface prep results at willitstick.fyi . Because every data point comes from this exact model, results are directly comparable across plates, materials, and brands; one shared test instead of a thousand private ones nobody can see. One short print, three answers 1. First-layer adhesion: did the first layer grip without sliding or lifting? 2. Warping: are the corners and long edges still flat when the print finishes? 3. Ease of removal : does it release cleanly once cool, without damaging the plate? Your result feeds the community adhesion matrix at willitstick.fyi ; crowdsourced, like-for-like data on which filaments stick to which build plates, with which surface prep. Every result comes from this exact model, so combos are actually comparable. Submitting takes about two minutes and no account: snap one photo, record pass/fail for the three checks at https://willitstick.fyi/submit . Full protocol (with photo examples) at https://willitstick.fyi/how-to-test ⚠️ Because this model is deliberately brutal, a failure doesn't mean your plate or filament is bad! It's a way to compare plate performance with evidence instead of feels. description: X2D Support Test – Multi-Material Support Benchmark Dieses Modell wurde speziell entwickelt, um die Qualität von Supportstrukturen und Multi-Material-Drucke objektiv zu bewerten. Durch die verschiedenen Überhänge, Aussparungen, Brücken und Kontaktflächen eignet sich der Test hervorragend, um die Druckqualität unterschiedlicher Materialkombinationen zu vergleichen und optimale Einstellungen für saubere Support-Oberflächen zu finden. Was wird getestet? Oberflächenqualität über Supportstrukturen Maßhaltigkeit kritischer Geometrien Qualität von Überhängen und Brücken Trennbarkeit der Supports Einfluss verschiedener Interface-Materialien Druckzeit und Materialverbrauch Vorteile von Multi-Material Supports Durch die Verwendung eines separaten Support-Interface-Materials lassen sich deutlich sauberere Unterseiten und Kontaktflächen erzielen als mit Supports aus dem gleichen Material. Besonders bei anspruchsvollen Überhängen können dadurch: glattere Oberflächen bessere Maßhaltigkeit weniger Nacharbeit einfachere Supportentfernung erreicht werden. Empfohlene Druckvarianten Variante 1 – Nur Support-Interface in anderem Material (empfohlen) Hier wird das Modell und die eigentlichen Supportstrukturen mit dem Hauptmaterial gedruckt. Lediglich die Support-Schnittstellen (Support Interface Layers) werden mit einem zweiten Material erzeugt. Beispiel: Modell: PLA Supports: PLA Support Interface: PETG Diese Methode bietet in der Regel das beste Verhältnis aus Druckqualität, Materialverbrauch und Druckzeit. Variante 2 – Komplette Supports in anderem Material Alternativ können sowohl die Supportstrukturen als auch die Support-Schnittstellen vollständig aus einem zweiten Material gedruckt werden. Beispiel: Modell: PLA Supports + Interface: PETG Diese Variante kann die Trennbarkeit weiter verbessern, erhöht jedoch den Materialwechsel erheblich. Wichtig: Durch die vielen Werkzeugwechsel zwischen den Materialien verlängert sich die Druckzeit deutlich und es entsteht zusätzlicher Materialabfall durch Spülvorgänge. Für die meisten Anwendungen ist daher Variante 1 die sinnvollere Wahl. Empfohlene Materialkombinationen PLA ↔ PETG PETG ↔ PLA ASA ↔ Support Material ABS ↔ Support Material Viel Spaß beim Testen! Teile gerne deine Ergebnisse, Einstellungen und Materialkombinationen in den Kommentaren, damit andere Nutzer von deinen Erfahrungen profitieren können. Hinweis Die Vorschaubilder und Darstellungen in diesem Eintrag wurden mithilfe von KI-generierten Grafiken erstellt und dienen ausschließlich der Veranschaulichung des Druckkonzepts. Das tatsächliche Druckergebnis kann je nach Drucker, Material und Einstellungen abweichen.

model_name: Printer test model when buying used printers 50g
description: Ever buy a used printer and not be confident that it works as advertised? Don't take that gamble! Send the seller this test model to run prior to you arriving, and request that they leave it on the build plate as proof that the printer works as advertised. There is no denying that the printer printed it, if its still stuck to the build plate when you arrive! This model is not a calibration model , it does not test over hangs, extrusion, nothing like that. This test was designed to make sure the printer can print most of the build plate, as well as show that the Z axis is clean and not bend. You can scale it up or down, but going too small will make that first layer pretty thin. I recommend scaling so the bottom is only 1 layer thick. That will show you how even the bed is and if the printer can print big flat models. The vertical part will show the z axis wear and tear, as well as show layer shifts, VFAs, ghosting and overall print quality. Check around the engraved letters for ghosting and VFAs, check around the corners to see proper extrusion and cornering and ringing, check the circle section to see if there are visible layer shifting. Finally check the pyramid top to ensure it can complete a top without knocking the entire model below over. Again, this is not a test of calibration, just a simple test model for you to be confident that the used printer you are buying can perform basic 3D printer tasks. I am uploading profiles for most current BambuLab Printers, as well as including the STL for other printers.

model_name: Parametric A1 PTFE Guide w. Ball Joint, for A1/A2L
description: Bambu A1 and A2L Swiveling PTFE Tube Guide - Parametric, with Print-in-Place Ball Joint If you've ever glanced over mid-print and noticed your drybox or your AMS Lite slowly sliding toward the print bed - pulled there by a taut filament tube - this one's for you. PTFE tube management is one of those details that seems trivial until it isn't. A loose or unsecured tube puts real tension on whatever it's attached to: a desktop spool holder, an AMS Lite, or a drybox on a shelf. Some existing guides rely on a dovetail joint or a friction fit that works fine in theory - until the repeated motion of printing slowly works the joint loose, and by the time you notice something is wrong, your setup has already been dragged somewhere it shouldn't be. I learned this the hard way so I designed my own. My design uses a fully print-in-place ball joint: it articulates freely so the tube always follows the print head without resistance, but the ball is physically captured inside the housing - there's no clip, no friction fit, nothing that can pull apart under load. The lever is printed horizontally so its strength doesn't rely on layer adhesion at all. And the C-clip uses a carefully angled opening that holds the tubes in place during normal use. Fully Parametric Configure four values to match your setup: Guide placement - top of the printer (usually for external spools) or towards the front (usually for a side-mounted AMS Lite) Guide diameter - size the C-clip to your tube count and diameter Lever length - a short lever works for most prints; increase it if you frequently print very tall models and need more slack Ball joint offset - position the guide towards the front, center, or back of the top bar Pre-configured standard variants are published alongside this model, so if your setup is typical you can go straight to printing without touching a single parameter. Printing note After printing, gently move the lever in the joint until it becomes loose and starts swiveling. Longer lever variants require a small horizontal bridge support under the lever. The included print profiles handle this automatically. Happy printing !

A dedicated storage case is also included to keep all the parts neatly organized when not in use. All parts can be printed on an A1 mini. Instructions 1. Assemble the Hand Crank The hand crank is assembled from three printed parts. The small hexagonal adapter is used when respooling with a ratchet wrench and a 10 mm socket. 2. Install the Holder on the AMS Lite Remove one rotary spool holder from the AMS Lite. Insert the printed inner holder onto the exposed AMS Lite shaft. This holder does not rotate, so the fitting is intentionally designed to be tight. 3. Install the Spools Screw the respooling core into the empty spool and tighten it securely. Install the empty receiving spool on the side fitted with the printed inner holder. Install the spool containing the filament on another spool holder of the AMS Lite. Pull out the filament and secure its end to the empty spool. 4. Respool the Filament For manual operation, attach the hand crank. When using an electric screwdriver, insert the hex driver bit fully into the drive socket. When using an electric drill, attach a 10 mm hex bit. When using a ratchet wrench, insert the included adapter and then attach a 10 mm socket. Important Notes An AMS Lite is required to use this model. This respooler does not include a mechanism for automatically distributing the filament evenly across the spool. model_name: Ultimate Top Layer Calibration (No Ironing Needed)
description: Tired of waiting hours for "Ironing" to finish, or dealing with the rough, inconsistent top surfaces on your prints? This comprehensive Top Layer Calibration Matrix helps you systematically find the perfect balance between Top Surface Line Width and Top Surface Speed for any filament. Dial in a flawless, smooth, and shiny top finish purely through optimized extrusion mechanics! This test utilizes a grid layout (Columns 1–5 and Rows A–K) featuring both flat rectangular sections and concentric circular test pads (as previewed in the slicer toolpath view). This allows you to evaluate how different settings handle straight infill lines versus tight, curved perimeters. How It Works (The Matrix Grid) The model is divided into a 5x11 grid matrix. Each cell modifies two critical variables to let you visually and texturally pick your winner: Columns (1 – 5): Top Surface Line Width 1: 0.30 mm 2: 0.35 mm 3: 0.40 mm 4: 0.45 mm 5: 0.50 mm Rows (A – K): Top Surface Speed A: 25 mm/s B: 50 mm/s C: 75 mm/s D: 100 mm/s E: 125 mm/s F: 150 mm/s G: 175 mm/s H: 200 mm/s I: 225 mm/s J: 250 mm/s K: 275 mm/s How to Use This Model Download & Slice: Open the provided .3mf file or arrange the model flat on your build plate. Apply Settings: Ensure you use a multi-modifier layout or a calibrated project file where each block/cell is mapped to its respective speed and width coordinates listed above or just hit SLICE without changing any parameters . Print & Inspect: Once printed, run your finger across the bed and tilt it under a strong light source. Look out for gaps between lines (under-extrusion/too narrow). Look out for rough ridges or scarring (over-extrusion/too wide or too fast). Save Your Profile: Find the single cell that looks perfectly smooth, flat, and uniform. Note its column and row values, and apply those exact settings to your favorite slicer profile!

description: This is a simple magnet fit tolerance test kit for common round magnets used in 3D printed projects. Instead of guessing the perfect hole size for your magnets, print the test strip that matches the magnets you have, press your magnets into the different holes, and choose the fit that works best for your printer, slicer settings, filament, and material. The kit includes separate test pieces for: 3×2 mm magnets 4×2 mm magnets 5×2 mm magnets 6×2 mm magnets 8×2 mm magnets 10×2 mm magnets Each size is a separate part, so you do not need to print the whole kit. Just print the strip for the magnet size you actually have. Each strip includes multiple hole diameters around the nominal magnet size, with the tolerance clearly labelled above each hole. For example, the 6×2 mm strip tests hole sizes from 5.95 mm to 6.25 mm. The magnet pockets are designed for 2 mm thick magnets. The back of each pocket is intentionally thin so the magnet can be pushed back out after testing. Why use this? Magnet fit can vary a lot depending on: Printer calibration Filament type Material shrinkage Nozzle size Slicer settings Hole compensation settings Whether you want a press fit, loose fit, or glue-in fit For best results, print the test strip in the same material you plan to use for your final project. For example, if your finished part will be PETG, print the test strip in PETG. If your final part will be ABS, print the test strip in ABS. Included sizes 3×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø2.95, Ø3.00, Ø3.05, Ø3.10, Ø3.15, Ø3.20, Ø3.25 4×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø3.95, Ø4.00, Ø4.05, Ø4.10, Ø4.15, Ø4.20, Ø4.25 5×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø4.95, Ø5.00, Ø5.05, Ø5.10, Ø5.15, Ø5.20, Ø5.25 6×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø5.95, Ø6.00, Ø6.05, Ø6.10, Ø6.15, Ø6.20, Ø6.25 8×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø7.95, Ø8.00, Ø8.05, Ø8.10, Ø8.15, Ø8.20, Ø8.25 10×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø9.95, Ø10.00, Ø10.05, Ø10.10, Ø10.15, Ø10.20, Ø10.25 Printing notes These are quick, simple prints and should not need supports. Recommended settings: Layer height: 0.16 mm or 0.20 mm Walls: 2 or more Infill: 10 to 20% Supports: No Brim: Not usually needed Orientation: Print flat on the build plate Material: Use the same material you plan to use for your final magnet project For the most accurate results, avoid scaling the model. 1 colour or 2 colour printing This model can be printed in either one colour or two colours . For a simple print, use one colour. The labels are still useful as raised or engraved text. For better readability, print the text in a second colour. A dark base with light text works especially well. How to use Choose the test strip that matches your magnet size. Print it in the material you plan to use for your final project. Press your magnet into each labelled hole. Find the fit you prefer. Use that hole diameter in your own CAD model. A tighter fit may work well for press-fit magnets. A looser fit may be better if you plan to use glue. Notes If you need a different magnet size, leave a comment. I can make additional sizes if people would like them.

The Ultimate Tracking Tower A weighted, magnetic, multi-angle reference tower designed to improve tracking stability during 3D scanning and photogrammetry. The Ultimate Tracking Tower creates a dense, three-dimensional field of black-and-white tracking markers around the scan volume. Rather than placing every marker on a flat sheet or directly on the turntable, the tower distributes reference points across a broad lower section, a raised central stem, and two faceted upper sections. This arrangement keeps usable markers visible from a wider range of scanner and camera positions. How It Works Users position the tower beside the object being captured or attach it directly to a magnetic turntable. During scanning, the system recognizes the visible markers as stable spatial references for tracking, pose estimation, and frame-to-frame alignment. The wide lower panels provide a large marker field near the turntable. The narrow stem raises additional reference points above the base without creating a large visual obstruction. The faceted upper sections present markers on several different planes and viewing angles. As the object rotates, or as the operator changes position, newly visible markers replace any that become hidden. This continuous marker coverage helps reduce tracking loss, alignment drift, repeated scan passes, and interruptions caused by target reacquisition. Advantages Over Conventional Marker Holders Flat marker boards provide reference points on only one plane and become less effective when the scanner moves outside their ideal viewing angle. Low-profile marker pucks can disappear behind taller objects. Simple cylindrical towers often place markers at similar angles and may provide limited geometric diversity. The Ultimate Tracking Tower addresses those limitations through: **Multi-height marker coverage.** Markers remain available near the turntable, beside the object, and above the object’s lower silhouette. * *Multi-angle visibility.** The faceted upper geometry presents targets toward several scanner positions instead of concentrating them on one flat surface. **Reduced object occlusion.** The narrow central stem raises markers while minimizing the amount of the object that the tower blocks. **A stable reference volume.** The combination of horizontal spread, vertical separation, and angular diversity provides the scanner with a stronger three-dimensional tracking reference than a flat board or basic marker post. **A weighted, magnetic base.** The base incorporates **four 2-inch-diameter by 4-mm-thick round magnets**. The magnets add useful weight, lower the center of gravity, and improve resistance to tipping. They also affix the tower securely to magnetic turntables, preventing unwanted movement during rotation while allowing users to reposition or remove the tower quickly. Recommended Finish The finished tower uses: SEM Products High-Build Primer Surfacer Part Number: 42013 Color: Gray This coating serves an optical and functional purpose, not merely a cosmetic one. Its high-build formulation helps fill and soften visible print-layer texture, while its sandable surface supports a cleaner final profile. The primer-flat finish also reduces concentrated reflections that can interfere with projected patterns, camera exposure, marker recognition, and optical measurement. Once the coating has fully cured, users can apply the required black-and-white tracking markers to the prepared surfaces. Why Medium Gray Is Better Than White or Black Many users assume that white or black must provide the best marker-tower color because those colors represent the brightest and darkest possible backgrounds. As general-purpose recommendations for structured-light scanning, laser scanning, and photogrammetry, both assumptions are wrong. White is too bright . Strong scanner illumination can make a white tower produce glare, clipped highlights, and excessive reflected light. A large white surface can drive automatic exposure downward, reduce available highlight headroom, and weaken separation from white marker centers or light-colored objects. Black is too dark . Black absorbs more projected light and returns a weaker optical signal. It can crush shadow detail, create tracking difficulties for optical systems, and visually merge with black plastic, rubber, carbon-look material, and other dark objects. Matte medium neutral gray provides the best overall balance . It is dark enough to control glare, light enough to remain visible to optical systems, and neutral enough to avoid unnecessary color bias. The midtone preserves more usable dynamic range than either white or black, supports more stable automatic exposure and white balance, and allows the black-and-white tracking markers to remain the dominant high-contrast features. For a general-purpose marker tower, the combination of **SEM 42013 High-Build Primer Surfacer, a matte gray finish, distributed marker geometry, and a weighted magnetic base** provides a more stable, versatile, and scan-friendly solution than conventional flat boards, unweighted towers, or extreme white and black finishes.

PWM 调光模块安装（右后方专属仓位） 增高架右后方为Type‑C进电区域，该位置自带带散热孔的独立小仓，专门放置调光模块； 在 PWM 模块背面打少量热熔胶，平整固定在仓内； 务必对准方向： 模块红外接收头朝外、对准散热孔 ，保证遥控器信号可以正常接收。 3. 走线、藏线与盖板安装 机身设计全隐藏走线结构，杜绝明线杂乱： 顶部带有一体式通线槽，所有灯线、按键线、供电线全部埋入线槽； 机器四角预留空心藏线仓（前左、前右、后左、后右），多余长线、多余元件全部可以收纳在四角空位； 灯带安装槽可用固定卡扣固定之后，在边缘有几个M2的螺丝孔，可使用 M2×6毫米的圆头螺丝 固定在外框，将灯带沿着槽贴入，然后 把灯带的线头从右前的槽口伸出 与PWM调光模块连接即可。 分区布局固定： 右前角：安装两个控制按键； 右后角：Type‑C 输入 + PWM 调光模块； 所有走线、元件固定完成后，盖上各位置盖板，并在上面粘贴好海绵条线路完全隐藏。 4. 电路接线方式（统一规范）！！ 接线逻辑简单规整、安全稳定： Type‑C 总输入接入后，所有负极全部并联汇总为公共负极； 正极分出两路，分别接入前面两个独立按键； 按键输出两路：一路给到 PWM 调光模块，再由调光模块连接至灯带； 另一路如果是X1/P1打印机用即可直接接到3010风扇， 若是X2D/P2S用则需预留好收纳在模块旁，用于后续拓展套件供电， 多余线头使用黑电工胶布全包绝缘。 5. 磁吸侧板安装 需要注意磁铁的极性！！ 建议盖板和底座各统一一种极性，可用502等类型的液体强力胶滴一点点在磁铁安装孔位，然后找准磁铁极性按入即可。 除X2D/P2S专用后部散热口和专用散热器使用直径6mm*高度6mm的磁铁（可买6*3版本的两个叠加用）外，其余的散热座和盖板均是采用5*2mm的钕磁铁，不要搞混型号 6. 底部收尾安装 整机装好后，在 线槽上整圈粘贴自带背胶海绵垫 ，起到防滑、减震作用，最后整体放置打印机顶部即可。 三、重点注意事项（必看） PWM 模块的红外接收头必须对准后方散热孔才可接收到外部遥控信号。 线路必须分路、负极统一共地 不要正负极乱分路，统一负极共地、正极按键分路，避免灯光闪烁、供电不稳。 P1/X1 装 3010 风扇款后板；P2S/X2D 使用原厂风扇专用风道后板，不要混用 X2D/P2S一路开关未接3010风扇，将线预留至右后方电路安装处，可用于后续扩展附件的安装（会开源） 备用线头必须绝缘胶带包裹，防止内部触碰短路。 磁吸盖板切勿硬扣暴力安装。 四、零件采购清单 必备基础件： ①强磁铁：5*2MM【至少52颗】+6*6MM【16颗】（X2D/P2S专用后散热口以及外排风扇需要，也可购直径6*高度3MM的两个堆叠用32颗） https://e.tb.cn/h.RJgeGydGK4qDIUr?tk=6UuMghNSSlU ② 螺丝：M4*16 +M2*6+ 螺母：M4标准螺母 ③5V LED 灯带：白光即可，https://e.tb.cn/h.RKSnqy40SADy8fO?tk=zKtGgh7l34h ④PWM 遥控调光模块一套：https://e.tb.cn/h.Rq33aFyfVxL1Cwe?tk=o72xgh7hpJV ⑤Type‑C 供电接口（如图同款） ：https://e.tb.cn/h.RrQPPN8MKnA3Cwq?tk=9ZMYgh7fSNM ⑥超短款自锁按键 ×2 （必须是超短款）12mm平头自锁两脚短款 ：https://e.tb.cn/h.RKSk9eGRWChhTU1?tk=dyJ5gh78gKo ⑦带背胶海绵贴条， 2cm宽2mm厚 ：https://e.tb.cn/h.RrKUSVDn9emWO0R?tk=6beYghNtGZJ ⑧电线、热熔胶、电工绝缘黑胶布若干\502类液体强力胶 机型专属配件（二选一） 3010双滚珠风扇11000转【5V ×3个】（P / X1 用户）：https://e.tb.cn/h.RrKuv6IedvH7NKn?tk=ww7jghnRALi 拓竹原厂 P2S / X2D 外排风扇组件， 安装详情及模型详见链接 ：https://makerworld.com.cn/zh/models/2656193-tuo-zhu-x2d-han-p2s-yuan-han-feng-shan-ding-bu-ci#profileId-3069641 拓展可选配件 堆叠式抽屉增高架， 安装详情及模型详见链接 ： 后续专属拓展套件（正在开发，开源，完成后会更新进来链接，可收藏一下后续进来看链接）

description: Give your Bambu Lab printer a retro gaming makeover! I couldn't find a PS Vita inspired bezel for my X2D or P2S, so I decided to design one myself. The goal wasn't just to make something that looked similar, it was to capture the proportions, spacing and overall feel of the original handheld while making it work naturally with the printer's touchscreen. The printer's display is slightly larger than the PS Vita's, so I chose to keep the bezel true to the console's proportions rather than shrinking the design and throwing off the iconic look. The result is a bezel that feels instantly recognisable while making the printer screen look like it was always meant to be there. The bezel simply snap-fits over the existing display with no modifications required. To maintain the authentic proportions of the original unit, the screen is intentionally tilted slightly upwards to provide enough clearance for the printer door to open. If you prefer to mount your screen flush against the printer, this design may not be suitable. However, I personally keep my screen slightly offset from the unit, so this has never been an issue for me. You still retain almost the full range of movement only the final portion of travel, when the screen is pushed completely flush against the printer, is lost. For me, preserving the correct proportions was well worth the small compromise. The shoulder buttons and camera lens are designed to be printed in a transparent filament for the best appearance, but they can also be printed in any colour you like. Whether you're a PlayStation fan, a retro gaming enthusiast or just want to personalise your printer, this is a fun little project that adds plenty of character without affecting everyday usability. As always, if you print one I'd love to see your setup! Feel free to upload your make, and if you think it's worthy of one, a Like, Download or Boost is always hugely appreciated. Printing Notes The shoulder buttons and camera lens are intended to be printed in transparent filament (optional) thay are coloured yellow in the studio. Install by simply snapping the bezel over the existing screen. Tilt the screen slightly upwards to allow the opening the printer door to prevent contact. Compatible with both the X2D and P2S.

Summary A spool holder designed to keep filament—especially TPU—dry while printing. It features a built-in desiccant (silica gel) container that continuously absorbs moisture during long prints. Weighing just over 400 g , it costs approximately $8 USD in filament to print. Deep Dive I designed this after running into a frustrating problem while 3D printing shoes in TPU. Each shoe took around 40 hours to print, and during that time the filament absorbed enough moisture to cause heavy stringing and failed prints. After purchasing a Bambu Lab AMS 2 Pro , I was able to dry my TPU, but since TPU can't be printed directly from the AMS, I had to move the spool back to the external holder on my A1 . Even after drying the filament for 12 hours , the print only stayed clean for the first couple of hours before moisture caused severe stringing again. I searched Maker World for a simple solution but couldn't find one that fit my needs, and I didn't want to buy additional hardware. So I designed my own. This spool holder has a desiccant container that goes in the hole in the middle of the spool, sealed with a screw-on lid. During printing, the silica gel continuously removes moisture from the air around the filament, helping keep it dry throughout the print. After installing this holder, I retried the print and the filament stayed dry for the entire 12–14 hour test print with excellent results. How to Use Feed the filament through the hole in the main body. Place the spool into the holder while keeping the filament threaded through the hole. Push the filament through your PTFE tube until it reaches the printer's toolhead. Insert the PTFE tube into the hole on the holder. About 1 mm of tubing should extend into the interior. Lay the holder on its side and funnel silica gel into the center compartment using a funnel. Screw the lid on securely. Do not overtighten. Stand the holder upright and start your print. Print Settings !!!Important!!!: This model has only been tested in PETG . Printing it in PLA or other materials is at your own risk. Also, avoid overtightening the lid regardless of the material used. Recommended settings: Material: PETG 3–4 walls minimum 10% infill is sufficient Gyroid infill is recommended, although any infill pattern should work Compatibility: Designed to fit most printers with exception of A1 mini Future Plans (V2) Once this model reaches 15 Boosts , I'll start designing Version 2 with: TPU gasket for a better seal Round hygrometer mounting slot Improved filament path and feeding I'm always open to suggestions, so if you have ideas for Version 2, let me know in the comments! Thanks! Thanks for checking out my model! I hope it helps others who struggle with keeping TPU dry during long prints. If you have any questions, feedback, or ideas for future improvements, feel free to leave a comment. I'd love to hear how it works for you!

Test completo del primo strato per Stampanti Bambu Lab (220x220 mm) Questo è un modello semplice ma fondamentale per verificare la perfetta calibrazione del piano di stampa e l'adesione del primo strato della vostra Stampante Bambu Lab . Il foglio copre l'intera area stampabile (220 mm x 220 mm) con uno spessore preciso di 0,2 mm (1 singolo strato). 🛠️ A cosa serve questo test? Verifica del livellamento del piano di stampa (Bed Leveling): consente di verificare a colpo d'occhio se il livellamento automatico della stampante funziona correttamente su tutta la superficie.
